all-s-well-that-ends-well-pg1529: Helena's dogged pursuit of the unwilling Bertram drives this edition of Shakespeare's bittersweet problem play. A bed-trick wins her the husband, but winning his love takes cunning, patience, and time. Darker than a comedy should be, it asks hard questions about desire and worth.
angus-religious-quests-1929:
Samuel Angus was an Australian scholar whose Religious Quests of the Graeco-Roman World appeared in 1929. The book studies the spiritual hungers of the ancient world on the eve of Christianity. Angus asks why the old civic cults left so many hearts unsatisfied.

He surveys mystery cults, astrology, magic, and the philosophies that promised rescue from fate and death. Converts, he shows, sought a savior, a sure hope after death, and a brotherhood that crossed nations. His account helps readers see the soil in which the early church grew, without preaching for or against it.
arxiv-2512-00029:
Connected devices now run urgent tasks across small edge units, local hubs, and distant cloud servers. Andreas Kouloumpris and three co-authors present an optimization framework, in a 2025 study, for deciding where each task should run. The setting differs from standard edge computing because it often uses one sensing edge device paired with one hub.

The framework aims to assign work across these layers in a clean, streamlined way so demanding applications run well. Such applications need fast responses and careful use of limited local hardware. For system designers, the study offers a structured way to split tasks among edge, hub, and cloud rather than sending everything to one place.
arxiv-2512-00129:
Deep learning systems can flag breast cancer in mammograms, but they often fail on images unlike their training data. Jayan Adhikari, Prativa Joshi, and Susish Baral tackle that reliability problem in a 2025 study. Scans from other modalities or different equipment can lead to wrong detections and misdiagnosis.

Their approach filters out-of-distribution inputs with a ResNet50-based stage, then detects cancer with YOLO models. Explainability methods and domain adaptation are part of the design. The goal is a screening tool that stays dependable when hospital equipment and imaging conditions change, instead of performing well only in the lab. Reliability under changed conditions is the theme that runs through the whole design.
arxiv-2512-00229:
Neural networks often fail silently when given inputs unlike anything in their training data. Suhail, Afroz, and Sethi present TIE in 2025, a framework for detecting such out-of-distribution inputs. The name stands for training, inversion, and exclusion, its three main stages.

Dependable systems need to estimate uncertainty and flag unfamiliar samples in a unified way, because overconfident predictions can be dangerous. TIE is designed to stay visually interpretable while it decides. The work matters for medical, driving, and security systems, where recognizing the unknown is as important as classifying the known. Interpretability is built into the framework's name and design, not added afterward. Uncertainty estimates give downstream systems a principled way to abstain.
arxiv-2512-00829:
Md Mehrab Hossain Opi, Sumaiya Khan, and Moshammad Farzana Rahman study faster training for Bangla language models in a 2025 paper. Training such models takes heavy computing power and long hours. In Bangla natural language processing, access to high-end hardware is often limited, so costs bite harder.

The team tests automatic mixed precision training. That method does much of the math in a lighter numeric format, while keeping key steps precise. Done right, it speeds training and saves memory without hurting model quality. Their work checks whether those savings hold for Bangla tasks, which would help local researchers do more with modest machines.
arxiv-2512-01029:
Vladimir Dragović and David Kalaj construct minimal surfaces over special quadrilaterals in a 2025 math paper. A Pitot quadrilateral has two pairs of opposite sides with the same total length, a property first tied to tangent circles. Minimal surfaces are shapes that locally minimize area, like soap films.

The authors build Scherk-type minimal graphs over any Pitot quadrilateral, with a fully explicit framework. First they produce a harmonic map from the unit disk onto the quadrilateral. Its stretching is the square of a Möbius map fixed directly by the quadrilateral's vertices. Explicit formulas make these surfaces computable, not just provable.
arxiv-2512-01629:
Yumeng He and co-authors rebuild articulated objects from a single photo for simulation. Objects with moving parts fill homes and workplaces. Robots need sim-ready models of them, with part trees and joints. Hand modeling those assets is slow expert work.

Their frame, SPARK, uses vision-language knowledge to infer parts. It outputs physically consistent, kinematic part models. Each part gets a place in a hierarchy with motion limits. One-photo assets could stock training worlds for robots far faster than hand modeling allows. Vision-language priors supply part names and joint guesses, which cuts the need for motion capture rigs in building each new asset.
arxiv-2512-02329:
Software engineering may be heading toward teams where autonomous AI agents do the core building, guided by human-set norms. Hoa Khanh Dam and four co-authors sketch in 2025 a new class of software engineering agents powered by large language models and equipped with beliefs, desires, intentions, and memory.

Such agents would reason about their work in a human-like way rather than merely completing tickets. The paper envisions autonomous normative multi-agent systems, teams of agents that also follow shared rules of conduct. It is a position paper, mapping how human-AI development teams could be reorganized around agents as primary drivers.
arxiv-2512-02429:
Algebraic geometers simplify complicated shapes by running the minimal model program, a sequence of surgeries toward a canonical form. Donghyeon Kim and Dae-Won Lee study in 2025 how that program behaves on the generic fiber of a fibration whose fibers are mostly of log Calabi-Yau type.

The setting assumes that over a dense set of the base, each fiber is a mildly singular log Calabi-Yau space. What the program does on the typical fiber governs the geometry of the whole family. Results here feed the classification of higher-dimensional varieties, where fibrations are the main tool for taking shapes apart.
arxiv-2512-02629:
C. Ramos Almeida and a large team study dust around feeding black holes using the James Webb telescope. Type-2 quasars hide their central black hole and inner gas behind thick dust and gas. Mid infrared spectra can still probe the dusty torus, the donut shaped cloud doing the hiding.

Webb's MIRI instrument recorded spectra from the centers of five nearby quasars of this type. Silicate emission in those spectra constrains the torus shape and how radiation pushes back on it. Better torus models sharpen our picture of how black holes grow inside their dusty cocoons. Dust that glows in this way tells on the shape of the cloud that hides the hole at its heart.
arxiv-2512-03229:
A combined galaxy catalog can tighten cosmic growth measures. H. Zou presents such a measure in this 2025 work, using the maximum likelihood fields method. The work joins three DESI first-release sources into one analysis.

The combined catalog holds hundreds of thousands of galaxy redshifts. It also holds tens of thousands of peculiar velocity measures from two distance methods. Blending both kinds of data gives a fuller picture of how matter moves. The resulting growth rate constraint helps test models of gravity and dark energy. Blending catalogs also cross-checks distance methods against each other in one frame.
arxiv-2601-06629:
Luis Croquevielle, Roman Sokolovskii, and Thomas Heinis bound learned index performance in 2026. Learned indexes speed queries by training models to approximate rank. A model predicts where a key sits in sorted data.

While effective in practice, their theoretical limitations are not fully understood. The authors present a general framework for proving lower bounds. Bounds are expressed in terms of the index's space overhead. They are parameterized by the model class used for approximation. Such bounds tell builders what no learned index can beat. Database researchers get a map of the possible, not just benchmarks. The framework separates clever engineering from hard mathematical limits cleanly. Future index designs can be judged against those limits directly.
arxiv-2601-07129:
Xinxin Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers minimum and extremal process for a branching random walk outside the boundary case. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. This work extends the studies on the minimum and extremal process of. A supercritical branching random walk outside the boundary case which cannot be reduced to the boundary case.

The authors study here the situation where the log-generating function explodes at 1 1. The random walk associated to the spine possesses a stretched exponential tail with exponent b b. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07429:
Research by Diogo Vieira Saraiva and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with tuning cholesteric cellulose nanocrystal self-assembly in spherical confinement via salt and sonication. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) self-assemble into cholesteric liquid crystals that produce structural color upon solvent removal.

Although most studies examine this process in planar films. Confinement within micron-sized water-in-oil droplets provides a powerful platform for resolving self-assembly dynamics in real time. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07629:
Valdemar Švábenský and colleagues review fifteen years of learning analytics research for the field's 2026 conference. Learning analytics studies data from learning settings to understand and improve education. The community recently marked its fifteenth conference and updated its 2011 definition. Yet little was known about how topics, funding, and collaboration have shifted together over time.

The authors map research topics and trends across that span, along with the challenges the field now faces. Linking topics to funding and collaboration shows who works on what, and with whom. Such a map helps a maturing field see its blind spots. New scholars can use it to find open ground. Funders and conference organizers also gain a clearer view of where the community is heading.
arxiv-2601-07729:
Luca M. Nashabeh and Liang Fu predict superconductivity in a two-layer system of electrons and holes. Their 2026 preprint studies density-balanced, mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayers. Experimenters can control carrier density and layer spacing separately in such systems. That control produces a rich phase diagram. It includes exciton condensates and Wigner crystals, among other phases.

For large hole-to-electron mass ratios, a new phase appears: an electron liquid beside a hole crystal. The authors examine where superconductivity can arise in this setting. Paired electron-hole systems are a long-standing route to unusual superfluid and superconducting states. A tunable platform lets theorists map cause and effect cleanly. The paper should interest condensed matter physicists who design layered quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-07829:
Atsushi Ueda and colleagues study how interfaces roughen inside a three-dimensional magnet model. Interfaces in many-body systems can fluctuate and host their own low-energy behavior, even when the bulk is gapped. The three-dimensional Ising model is the test bed. Their 2026 preprint uses tensor networks, a numerical method that compresses quantum and statistical states efficiently. Interface roughening is the shift from a flat boundary to a wandering one.

That shift is a phase transition in its own right. Tensor networks let the authors probe it with controlled accuracy. The physics connects to crystal growth, wetting, and surface ordering. Understanding one clean model guides intuition for many real surfaces. The paper speaks to statistical physicists who study phase transitions. It also shows tensor networks at work outside their usual quantum setting.
arxiv-2601-08029:
Andrey Kardashin and Konstantin Antipin study how measurement choice changes the variance of quantum neural networks. Variational quantum circuits perform machine learning tasks on labeled quantum states. In some tasks, and for some circuit designs, measurements cover only part of the input state. That restriction is their focus. Their 2026 preprint analyzes measurement-dependent variance in these networks.

Variance decides whether a quantum model's training signal survives or drowns in noise. If gradients vary too wildly or vanish, training fails. Measurement choice is a design lever that practitioners control directly. Understanding its effect helps set up trainable circuits. The paper serves quantum machine learning scholars. It studies a specific, practical source of training difficulty rather than the general barren plateau story.
arxiv-2601-08129: Roland Rodriguez Jr. proposes pressure fields as a way for agent systems to coordinate without a central manager. His 2026 arXiv paper notes that current multi-agent language model frameworks copy human org charts. Planners delegate to executors, and managers coordinate workers in fixed hierarchies. Such control adds overhead that scales poorly as agent count and task complexity grow. Rodriguez instead lets coordination emerge from pressure fields with temporal decay. The idea aims at leaner teamwork among many software agents on shared tasks.
arxiv-2601-08629: Saumitra Yadav and Manish Shrivastava argue for source-side data curation in low-resource machine translation. Their 2026 arXiv paper calls curation a critical yet under-researched step in training translation systems. Training data comes mainly from human translations and digital parallel sources, with limited synthetic generation. For low-resource languages, human translation at scale is prohibitively expensive. Curating the source side well could yield usable parallel corpora with less data. Their title puts it plainly: get away with less by choosing source text with care.
arxiv-2601-08729:
Jinhan Kim and four co-authors take a close look at a test rule for deep neural nets. The rule is called Neural Coverage, or NLC for short. Yuan and his team put it out in 2023. They said it met eight design goals and did well in tests. Kim and his team ask if those claims hold up.

The team checks both the math claims and the test claims. They say some of the base claims need a fresh look. Their point is not just about one rule. How we test a net shapes how safe we think it is. A reader who builds or tests such nets gets a clear warn to check coverage rules with care.
arxiv-2601-08929:
Zachary Robertson asks when a table of shared facts between traits is a sound table in a strict math sense. Each cell in the table holds a shared fact score for a pair of traits. The score can be built in more than one way, based on a curve that sets how gaps count. A sound table here means one with no bad eigen traits, called PSD for short.

He gives a local test that tells which curves yield sound tables. The test rests on how the curve acts near the point where two traits match in full. Such tables show up in learn tools that use shared fact as a link gauge. A reader gets a crisp rule for when that gauge is safe to use as a base.
arxiv-2601-09029:
Aniesh Chawla and Udbhav Prasad test chat models as early warn scouts for cyber threats. Most bad code hunts are reactive: they wait for a known bad file. A scout reads loose web text on new threats and pulls out signs of risk, such as bad hosts or file prints. Such signs let a firm block a threat before it hits.

The pair give the first broad test of chat models on this scout task. They check if models can pull true signs from noise and hype. False signs waste staff time, so care counts as much as reach. A reader in cyber work gets a first scale for AI scouts. It shows if they can aid a guard team, or just add noise.
arxiv-2601-09329:
Jun Su, Guangyue Han, and Shlomo Shamai build a code plan for channels with memory, based on a famed old plan. The old plan, by Schalkwijk and Kailath, sends a value by a loop that zooms in on it with each round. It is known for vast gains on a plain noise channel. Real channels hold memory: past noise bends next noise in a set way.

Their plan, called SK(2), fits that memory case for a class of such channels. They give a closed form for the rate it can reach. A code with a form, not just a bound, can be built and run. A reader in comms work gets a zoom loop code for channels as they are, not as we wish.
arxiv-2601-09429:
Abraão J. S. Capistrano and three co-authors test whether Nash gravity can stand in for the standard cosmology. Their 2026 arXiv paper checks the model against baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey. Nash gravity grows out of Nash's embedding theorem, which views spacetime inside a higher-dimensional space.

In this model, wiggles in the extrinsic curvature create scalar perturbations directly from geometry. No extra fields need to be added by hand. The authors ask whether the resulting universe matches the pattern DESI measures in galaxy clustering. Tests like these decide whether a modified gravity idea stays a curiosity or becomes a rival.
arxiv-2601-09529:
Fatemeh Kayanikhoo, Mateusz Kapusta, Miljenko Čemeljić, and Leszek Zdunik model stars made of strange quark matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the first of a pair, asks how heavy and how deformed such a star can be. The stars spin and carry strong magnetic fields.

The matter follows the MIT bag model with a density-dependent bag constant. The authors include Landau quantization for fields up to 5×10^17 gauss inside the star. Spin rate and field strength together set the star's mass and shape. If strange quark stars exist, these limits tell observers what to look for.
arxiv-2601-10129:
Linquan Wu and co authors fix a gap in how small sight models learn from large ones. A small model may copy the words of its teacher. Yet it may look at the wrong part of the image. It then leans on word habits, not on true sight.

The team names this the Perception Gap. Their fix lines up the inner sight of the pupil with that of the teacher. The pupil learns where to look as it learns what to say. The work is named LaViT. It treats sight paths as part of the skill to pass on.
arxiv-2601-10529:
Vladimir Petrov Kostov takes up three build asks for real polynomials. Each has one variable and no zero terms. Its terms have signs that form a pattern. A build ask goes the other way. Given a sign pattern, can a polynomial with it be built?

Kostov works on three such asks. The pattern is read from the top term down to the fixed term. Each ask adds its own binds on the terms. The paper seeks which patterns can occur and which can not. Such asks tie sign facts to root facts in a sharp way.
arxiv-2601-10729:
Xinyue Ma and co-authors present OrbitFlow, a serving system for long-context language models. Serving such models is tricky because request lengths and batch mixes shift while text is generated. Memory use swings with them. Moving key-value caches to host memory helps, but fixed offloading plans cannot keep up with the swings.

OrbitFlow reconfigures the cache at a fine grain while watching service-level goals. The aim is to meet response targets without wasting scarce accelerator memory. Static plans either hoard memory or stall requests. An adaptive plan can do better on both counts. The work speaks to data centers that run long-document chat and analysis under tight latency promises.
arxiv-2601-11629:
Nghia Le, Alan Ritter, and Kartik Goyal watermark low-entropy model outputs. Their 2026 preprint presents SeqMark, a sequence-level algorithm. Watermarking marks AI text so its origin can be checked. Current methods work well for open-ended generation tasks.

Constrained tasks have low-entropy output spaces to choose from. Code, forms, and short answers leave little room to hide marks. Standard watermarks prove inadequate in that tight space. SeqMark uses semantic differentiation at the sequence level. It balances output quality with watermark detectability. Imperceptibility, not standing out to readers, is the third goal. The balance matters where outputs must stay exact.
arxiv-2601-11729:
Turhan Can Kargin, Wojciech Jasiński, Adam Pardyl, Bartosz Zieliński, and Marcin Przewięźlikowski built a test for space sense in large vision models. Models such as DINO and CLIP read the sense of an image well. Yet they are weak at space tasks, such as judging depth or place, which robots need.

Their test, named SpaRRTa in the work, is made from fake scenes built by code. It lets them check space skills in a clean, set way. Recent work adds 3D tasks to model training, so a fair test is now key. The test can show where a model still fails at space thought.
arxiv-2601-12329:
Mithlesh Singla, Seema Kumari, and Shanmuganathan Raman work on a core task in image work. The task splits one image into two parts. One part is albedo, the base color of a surface. The other part is shading, the light and dark laid over that color.

Such splits help with tasks like relighting a scene or changing how a surface looks. Past models do this well, but they tend to be large. A large model is costly to pair with other tools in real use. Their method, called FlowIID, does the split in a single step. It uses latent flow matching to keep the cost down.
arxiv-2601-12429:
Martin Dindos, Linhan Li, and Jill Pipher work on a class of heat type equations. Their equation is parabolic, with a term that spreads and a term that flows in time. They impose zero Neumann data, a boundary rule on the flow across the edge. The setting is a Lipschitz cylinder, a domain with rough sides.

The team prove a localization estimate for local solutions of this problem. Their proof assumes that two linked problems can be solved in set ranges. One is the Neumann problem for the main operator, and the other is the Dirichlet problem for its adjoint. Estimates of this kind let global facts be built from local ones. They are core tools in the modern theory of partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-12829:
R. W. Fearick and five co authors measure electric dipole strength in light nuclei. Total photoabsorption cross sections matter for nuclear structure and for astrophysics. Most data come from neutron emission after photoexcitation of a nucleus. In heavy nuclei, that emission approximates the total cross section well.

The team turn to sd shell nuclei, a lighter class of nuclei. They use small angle proton scattering to extract the dipole strength instead. Proton scattering at tiny angles can mimic a photon probe with fine control. Better strength data feed models of how stars forge elements. They also test nuclear theory in a regime where calculations are feasible.
arxiv-2601-13229:
Shreyes Nallan and Jian-Gang Zhu build a computing frame that can run both ways. In such a frame, logic gates are swapped for a net of linked chance bits. The net is two way by build. It can work out outputs from inputs, or work back to inputs from a set output.

That two way trait suits hard tasks. It can draw random samples fast. It can run new kinds of rules. It also fits tasks such as split a number into prime parts. Their frame is driven by how current steers tiny magnet tools that talk to each other. The work moves chance based computing from maths toward real hardware.
arxiv-2601-13629:
Ziqian Wang, Xianjun Xia, Chuanzeng Huang, and Lei Xie present a singing style transfer system in 2026. Their system, S2 Voice, won both tracks of the Singing Voice Conversion Challenge of 2025. One track used known singers, and the other used new voices with no prior samples. The base is a two-stage system called Vevo.

S2 Voice adds stronger control of style and more robust output. Style here means the tone, flair, and feel of a singer's voice. Good control lets a song keep its tune while sounding like a new singer. The win marks the system as a top tool for this task.
arxiv-2601-13729:
Weichuan Wang, Mingyang Liu, Linqi Song, and Chen Ma study how random output shapes machine translation in 2026. Language models do not always give the same reply to one prompt. That non-deterministic trait sways real tools in clear ways. In translation, a complex task, this trait has been little explored.

The team tests modern translation systems in a systematic way. They pin down temperature-constrained non-deterministic translation as its own phenomenon. Temperature is the dial that sets how wild the model's choices get. Naming and gauging the effect is a first step to taming it for users.
arxiv-2601-13829:
Makafui Avevor, Hossein Safi, and co-authors model light links between small satellites in 2026. Modulating retroreflectors offer a low-complexity path for CubeSat optical links. A retroreflector bounces light back to its source, and modulation stamps data on it. The setup is asymmetric, with one side doing most of the work.

The team builds a unified statistical channel model for these links. It captures pointing losses, both random and fixed, and signal-dependent noise. They also optimize the design and benchmark it against other options. Cheap, low-power links could let swarms of small satellites share data.
arxiv-2601-14229:
David Seery, a cosmologist, wrote this 2026 paper on the early universe. It deals with inflation, the fast stretch thought to have shaped the young cosmos. He asks how very short waves from that era push back on one long, smooth wave. In math terms, the long wave is an adiabatic mode. The short waves here have large size.

Seery works through a loop expansion of the long-mode power spectrum. In that count, the push-back first shows up at one loop. He uses the separate universe method, which treats each patch of space as its own small cosmos. The scale gap between long and short waves makes that method a clean fit for the task.
arxiv-2601-14529:
Juan J. Segura compares reacting porous-flow systems across scale in this 2026 paper. His emphasis is hydrometallurgical heap leaching, where liquid is trickled through ore heaps to extract metal. He develops a unified, dimensionless framework for geometrically similar systems. Under dynamic similarity, the dimensionless liquid residence-time distribution is identical across scales.

Real systems break that neat picture. Differences in particle size distribution and intraparticle pore structure break microscopic similarity. The title names his tools: PSD-distributed Damköhler numbers and dual-porosity flow. The scale jump is the hard part. What works in a jar of ore may fail in a heap the size of a hill. Readers get a framework for saying when a lab column truly predicts a full heap, and when it cannot.
arxiv-2601-14829:
Héctor Cancio and Pere Masjuan present a holographic model of QCD in this 2026 paper. The talk was given at the QCD25 conference in Montpellier. Through the model, they study the running of the strong coupling constant in both non-perturbative and perturbative regimes. The model is a double dilaton soft-wall model. Renormalization of the metric tensor is driven by the Ricci Flow.

The breaking of conformal and chiral symmetries, thanks to the double dilaton and large-N corrections, links two facts. An infrared fixed point in the coupling constant connects with a smooth matching between regimes. The title also names pion form factors at intermediate energies. Readers get phenomenology that ties deep theory to a measurable pion trait.
arxiv-2601-15229:
Franz Lemmermeyer links a famous contest problem to the theory of number fields. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with Vieta jumping, a proof trick named for the way solutions leap from one to another. The trick is best known from a problem set at the 1988 olympiad.

That problem is widely seen as one of the hardest ever set at the event. Lemmermeyer explains its tie to elements of small norm in quadratic number fields. Parametrized units in those fields supply the hidden structure. The article lays the connection out step by step.
arxiv-2601-15429:
Sydney Anuyah, Mehedi Mahmud Kaushik, and co-authors test whether knowledge graphs make medical chatbots more trustworthy. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with large language models in health care. The models answer fluently but can fail at domain-specific reasoning.

The team builds three graphs from PubMed papers. One covers type 2 diabetes, one Alzheimer's disease, and one both diseases together. They test whether these graphs improve retrieval-augmented generation. In that setup, the model reads retrieved facts before it answers. The three graphs supply structured, checked facts for the retrieval step to use well.
arxiv-2601-15929:
Liuyun Jiang and four co-authors outline neurons with a new network design in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neuron maps are the base for rebuilding connectomes. Connectomes show how the brain is wired and how it works. Neurons have odd shapes and dense, tangled forms. That makes them hard to outline. CNN methods often miss faint edges for lack of wide context. Transformer methods lose fine voxel detail, which blurs edges the other way.

Their model is NeuroMamba. It uses visual Mamba blocks to mix features from many views. Mamba models handle long sequences at less cost than transformers. Mixing views aims to keep both context and fine detail. In dense brain scans, one edge error can merge or split a neuron in the wrong place. Better outlines speed the whole connectome pipeline.
arxiv-2601-16529:
Dongshen Peng and three coauthors test if models cave to sick case push in ER sims. Their 2026 preprint, named SycoEval-EM, deals with aid models in care. Such models may agree with a case who begs for wrong care. That cave in, called sycophancy, can cause real harm in ER work. The team builds a sim with more than one agent to test it.

Foe case agents push for care that is not apt. Tests span a wide set of ER case tales. Cave rates show which models hold firm on true care. Firm holds are a must ere ward use can be safe. The work gives a test for that firm hold.
arxiv-2601-16629:
Stef Accou and Wessel Poelman group adapter terms by tongue type to save train cost. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that serve many tongues. Such models lag on low stock and new tongues most. Adapters, small add parts per tongue, fix lag at less cost. Yet one adapter per tongue still costs much at full scale.

Type led groups let kin tongues share adapter terms in part. Shared terms cut train cost while they keep tongue skill. Type facts come from tongue build and past links. The work seeks cheap skill for tongues left behind. It tests groups as the unit of adapter craft.
arxiv-2601-17229:
Jarosław Pawłowski, Piotr Surówka, and Konstantin Zarembo study electron flow in very clean flat materials. In such materials, electrons flow more like a fluid than like lone charges. Viscosity matters as much as plain resistance. The authors use Brinkman equations, a simple frame for such fluid-like flow. They ask what sharp obstacles do to the current.

They find a geometric skin effect. Near sharp edges, the current grows stronger. Far from the edges, where flow is free, the current drops. Shape alone can thus reshape where charge moves. The result matters for tiny devices built from clean materials. It shows that layout is part of the physics, not just packaging.
arxiv-2601-17329:
Tiejin Chen and four co-authors study how to align language models with human feedback. The standard method learns from pairs. A person picks the better of two answers. Those picks can be noisy and at odds. Past fixes weigh each pair by how sure it seems. The authors say a deeper point is missed. The answers in the pair vary in how much they can be trusted at all.

Their method, Conformal Feedback Alignment, scores that answer-level trust. Alignment then leans on pairs whose answers hold up. Cleaner training signals should give safer, more true models. The work speaks to any team that trains models on human picks.
arxiv-2601-17429:
Mehdi Yousefzadeh and four co-authors tackle vessel maps in X-ray angiography. That imaging is the clinical standard for coronary artery disease. Yet measuring vessels in routine scans is hard. Low contrast, motion, and overlap blur the arteries. Catheters add false shapes. Centers also differ, which shifts the data. The team works on two tasks at once.

They segment the coronary arteries from the background. They also classify vessel type along the tree. Both tasks must hold up in real clinic data. Good maps guide stent and surgery choices. Robust tools could cut the hand work that slows reads. The study targets the flaws that block daily use.
arxiv-2601-17529:
Fengting Zhang and five co-authors present FMIR, a medical image registration framework. Registration aligns scans so they can be compared. Deep learning made it fast, yet models fail on new domains. Medical sets are small, so that flaw bites hard. FMIR builds on a foundation model to widen its reach. The design aims to keep speed while gaining range.

A tool that works across hospitals saves lives and time. Scans differ by machine, site, and patient group. Broad registration supports surgery plans and disease tracking. Foundation models bring broad prior knowledge to the task. FMIR tests if that breadth solves the domain gap. The clinic, not the benchmark, is the real judge.
arxiv-2601-17629:
Meysam Babapour and Ehsan Taheri design robust low-thrust spacecraft trajectories. Low-thrust engines push gently for long spans. Plans must hold up under random disturbances. The authors use chance-constrained covariance steering. One key point is spacecraft mass change. Mass shifts affect thrust acceleration. They also affect how strong disturbances feel.

Both levels of mass effect enter the design. A covariance form keeps the math efficient. Robust paths save fuel and cut mission risk. Deep-space missions cannot be re-flown if plans fail. The method gives planners a systematic path. It treats doubt as part of the route, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-17729:
Zihan Pengmei presents cuGUGA, a new solver for a hard task in quantum chemistry. The 2026 preprint deals with configuration interaction, a method that builds the state of a system from many simpler states. The solver works in a basis that keeps spin symmetry built in from the start. It runs on graphics hardware through CUDA, the platform for such chips.

Two design choices keep the solver fast. Counts of paths through a graph are precomputed, so ranking states takes a fixed, short time. Segment factors are also stored in tables ahead of time. That makes the coupling terms quick to evaluate as well. The result is a tool aimed at larger and harder chemistry problems.
arxiv-2601-17829:
Dan Greenstein, Zohar Karnin, Chen Amiraz, and Oren Somekh study how to make training data for tool-using AI agents more varied. Their 2026 preprint is about function-calling agents, systems that pick and fill software functions to get tasks done. Good training data is a main bottleneck for such agents. Past work varied the functions, the call patterns, and the turns of talk.

Two gaps got less care: how requests are worded, and which argument values appear. A request can name a city or a stock code in many ways. If training data is too samey, agents stumble on real user phrasing. The authors target that language and argument spread head-on. Wider spread should make agents hardier in live use.
arxiv-2601-17929: Tarik Aougab, Hikaru Jitsukawa, and Kim Ruane write an elementary primer on the quasi-isometric rigidity of the integers. Their 2026 preprint sits in geometric group theory. The text also serves as a tribute to Chatawate (Flame) Ruethaimetapat, a young scholar in the field who died in August 2024. The primer keeps the tools basic so new readers can follow the proof ideas.
arxiv-2601-18029:
Kengo Deguchi, Haider Munawar, and Runjie Song derive simple tests for when a swirling flow stays calm. Their 2026 preprint studies inviscid shear instability in axisymmetric flows. The base flows run in annuli and pipes. The authors seek plain criteria that say whether such a flow is stable or will break into disturbance. They treat both symmetric and non-symmetric disturbance types.

Their sufficient condition for stability sharpens a classical result. It builds on the second Kelvin-Arnold stability theorem. Simple, sound tests save heavy computation in design work. Flows in pipes and rings sit inside engines, reactors, and lab rigs, so the tests have wide reach.
arxiv-2601-18129:
Kunat Pipatanakul and Pittawat Taveekitworachai present Typhoon-S, an open effort to give smaller language communities their own large models. Their 2026 preprint notes a skew in the field. Top models are trained and tested mostly in high-resource languages like English and Chinese. They are also built by a few groups with huge compute and data. Sovereign models aim to break that dependence for other nations and tongues.

The authors describe a minimal, open post-training recipe. Minimal means the steps are kept few and clear, so others can copy them. Open means the results can be checked and reused. The work serves countries that want AI in their own language, on their own terms.
arxiv-2601-18429:
Corentin Barloy and three colleagues study how small logic rules can keep track of sets of words as they change. The frame is a live one: a word list is kept up to date while bits flip one by one. A rule set counts as fit if it can state, after each flip, which words still pass a fixed test. Past work showed the full set of plain word tests can be kept in this way.

The team sort the word tests into finer ranks. For each rank they ask what kind of maths the rules must hold to stay in step. Their ranks use forms from algebra, the study of sets with rules for join and swap. The work ties two fields that seem far apart: the shape of words and the shape of change. That tie may help in checks on live data streams.
arxiv-2601-19029:
An unnamed author argues that piano playing should be judged from sound, not just from note data. Scores in MIDI form list which notes were hit and when, but they miss the tone and touch that make playing expressive. The author instead uses audio foundation models, large models trained on sound itself.

Two such models, MuQ and MERT, feed a system that scores many sides of performance quality. The target list spans a wide set of traits that listeners hear. If sound based scores beat note based ones, teachers and exam tools gain a judge that hears what an audience hears.
arxiv-2601-19129:
Puzhen Wu and eight co-authors fix badly exposed photos with help from a vision language model. Poor exposure wipes out detail, shifts colors, and flattens contrast. Fixes face two snags. They ignore what each object in the scene is, which causes odd color shifts. And real photos rarely come with a corrected twin to learn from.

Their method is unsupervised and aware of scene meaning, guided by CLIP. Object aware fixes can treat sky, skin, and shadow in ways that suit each one. Work that needs no hand made ground truth can scale to the messy photos people truly take.
arxiv-2601-19229:
Benling Li and Wei Zhao report analytic facts on Finsler manifolds that break Riemannian habits. Finsler geometry lets distance depend on direction, a looser frame than the Riemannian one. In the Riemannian world, every flat Cartan-Hadamard manifold is just Euclidean space in disguise.

That sameness underlies the sharpness of key inequalities, like Hardy's and the uncertainty principle. On Finsler manifolds, the pair find phenomena with no Riemannian twin. Such surprises warn analysts about tools built for the classic setting. Those tools may fail, or change meaning, when direction starts to matter. The pair mark the exact spots where the old intuition gives way.
arxiv-2601-19729:
Aldo Gardini and Lorenzo Mori work on a measurement problem in public health. Health surveys sample few people in each small area, so direct estimates for those areas are noisy. Small area estimation borrows strength across areas to sharpen the numbers. The authors apply these methods to mapping smoking behaviour.

Their outcome data come from self-reports, which suffer from coarsening. People round answers and favour certain digits, blurring the true values. Ignoring that blur can bias the maps. The authors build a Bayesian two-part model that handles coarsened data directly. Better local estimates help target anti-smoking programs where they are needed most. The method suits other self-reported health measures too.
arxiv-2601-19829:
M. Khodas, Libor Šmejkal, and I. I. Mazin explore superconductivity in a newly recognised kind of magnet. P-wave magnets have no net magnetisation, yet their electron bands split by spin in a non-relativistic way. That combination resembles altermagnets, another recent class of magnetic materials. The spin polarisation in these systems points in a fixed direction across momentum space.

The authors discuss whether such magnets can host superconductivity, and of what kind. They call the possibility nonrelativistic-Ising superconductivity. Pairing in a spin-split band structure should differ sharply from ordinary superconductors. If realised, it could yield devices that marry magnetism with zero-resistance current. The paper maps the theoretical ground for experimentalists to test.
arxiv-2601-20029:
Enhyeok Jang and six colleagues cut the training cost of a quantum optimization algorithm. QAOA tackles combinatorial problems by alternating quantum operations tuned by classical parameters. Its multi-angle variant gives every Hamiltonian term its own parameter. That freedom improves answers with fewer layers, but the parameter count inflates classical training cost.

Their cyclic layerwise training scheme organises the optimization to tame that cost. Training proceeds layer by layer in a repeating cycle. The scheme aims to keep multi-angle quality while restoring practicality. Optimization problems from logistics to finance motivate the algorithm. Cheaper training decides whether such quantum methods ever leave the lab. The cost is paid in plain cash and time.
arxiv-2601-20329:
A. Rahmatinejad, T. M. Shneidman, and N. Jovancevic calculate level densities for two plutonium isotopes, split by parity. Level density counts how many quantum states a nucleus has at a given energy. The authors track the ratio between positive and negative parity across a broad range of shapes, from spherical to strongly deformed.

Their range covers both the ground-state shape and the second minimum, the fission isomer. They compare the energy at which the two parities reach equilibrium between these shapes. Such densities feed into models of fission and neutron capture, where the nucleus passes through its deformed states.
arxiv-2601-20429:
Junseo Lee and four colleagues present GRTX, an efficient ray tracing method for rendering scenes built from 3D Gaussians. Gaussian splatting renders scenes fast and with high quality, but most systems use rasterization, which projects shapes onto the screen. Rasterization has fundamental limits, such as trouble with reflections and complex light paths.

Ray tracing can handle those effects but is costly on Gaussian scenes. GRTX aims to make it practical. Efficient ray tracing would let Gaussian scenes gain realistic lighting and shadows while keeping their speed edge, a gain for games, simulation, and virtual production.
arxiv-2601-20529:
Julia Richter and a large team set out a practical framework of key performance indicators for multi-robot field tests on the Moon and other planets. Robots will prospect for resources such as ilmenite, rare earth elements, and water ice. Analog field trials pursue these goals, but their results are hard to compare because platforms and setups differ so much.

The authors propose shared indicators so trials can be measured on common ground. Common measures would let space agencies and teams learn from each other's tests instead of starting over. That speeds the path to robots that can scout the Moon reliably.
arxiv-2601-20829:
Minwu Kim, Safal Shrestha, and Keith Ross tackle a stall in training reasoning models. Their 2026 paper studies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. That method has greatly improved the reasoning of large language models. But training stalls once problems become saturated. Saturated problems are ones the model now almost always solves. They stop teaching it anything new.

The authors name the core issue: informative failures are hard to reach. The learning signal lives in failed attempts, yet standard rollouts rarely produce them. Their fix is failure-prefix conditioning. Training starts the model from the front part of a failed attempt. From there, useful failures become common again. The method aims to keep hard training sets useful for longer.
arxiv-2601-20929:
Wendy Sun, Rohan Naidu, and a large team argue that the centers of Little Red Dots are a new kind of object. Their 2026 paper studies these compact red sources, seen by JWST in the early universe. Their central engines may be black hole stars. Such a star is an early stage of black hole growth wrapped in dense gas. The best evidence comes from a few sources.

In those sources, the host galaxy is fully outshone. Their spectra show steep Balmer breaks, a mark of dense gas. The title's sums state the claim: take away the host, and a black hole star remains. The authors propose one at the center of each Little Red Dot. If right, this rewrites how the first black holes grew.
arxiv-2601-21029:
Samuel Stanek and four co-authors study a flaw that dims a fast laser scanner. Their 2026 paper concerns electro-optical deflectors made from KTN crystals. These deflectors steer laser beams with unmatched speed. They serve laser-scanning microscopy and other applications. Their weakness is a limited deflection range. KTN devices offer some of the highest counts of resolvable spots. They work by fields from trapped electrons inside the crystal.

The paper examines photoionization in these deflectors. The light used lies in the near-infrared imaging window. Ionization by that light can disturb the trapped charge that steers the beam. Understanding the effect is key to wider, steadier scans. The study joins materials physics with instrument design. It helps builders of fast microscopes push their range.
arxiv-2601-21529:
Robert van der Klis, Ricardo Chávez Torres, Max van Spengler, Yuhui Ding, Thomas Hofmann, and Pascal Mettes build fast neural networks that live in hyperbolic space. That curved space suits data with tree-like structure, such as categories and family trees. A sound math base for networks in this space has been slow to arrive.

The authors give a formulation that is both efficient and faithful to the geometry. Their networks use the Lorentz model, prized for numerical stability. Fast, correct hyperbolic layers could lift tasks from language hierarchies to recommendation, where tree shapes are everywhere but flat models flatten them away.
arxiv-2601-21629:
Daniel Mills, Ifan Williams, Jacob Swain, Gabriel Matos, Enrico Rinaldi, and Alexander Koziell-Pipe teach a learner to order quantum circuit optimizations. Quantum toolkits ship many optimization passes, each well tested on its own. The order in which passes run, though, is left to the user or to a generic default.

The authors use reinforcement learning to compose pass sequences for each circuit. A good order for one circuit can be poor for another, so adapting per circuit beats one fixed recipe. Better ordering means smaller, faster circuits. That helps today's small quantum machines, where every saved operation counts.
arxiv-2601-21729:
A.Ya. Maltsev studies whether extremely complex conductivity diagrams can arise in metals with cubic symmetry. The analysis uses the nearly free electron approximation, a standard first model of electrons in a crystal. Conductivity diagrams map how current responds as conditions vary.

Estimates show that ultra-complex diagrams need the Fermi level to land in very narrow energy windows inside the conduction band. Such windows are rare, which explains why the wildest diagrams are seldom seen. The result still maps where to look. It guides experiments on pure cubic metals that hunt for extreme magnetotransport behavior.
arxiv-2601-21829:
Bsher Karbouj, Baha Eddin Gaaloul, and Jörg Krüger present a dataset built to measure mental workload where people work beside robots. Their 2026 paper describes GAZELOAD, a multimodal dataset gathered in a laboratory assembly testbed designed to mimic industrial human and robot collaboration.

Twenty-six participants worked with two collaborative robots, a UR5 and a Franka Emika Panda, while wearing smart glasses that tracked their eyes. Eye movements offer clues about attention and strain that self-reports miss. A shared dataset like this lets researchers train such systems. It also lets them compare systems fairly. The goal is factories that respond when a worker is overloaded. Such a factory could slow down, warn, or offer help.
arxiv-2601-21929:
Shuangqi Li, Hieu Le, Jingyi Xu, and Mathieu Salzmann ask which training examples shaped a model's answer. Training data attribution answers that question, and the best methods use gradients to define an influence function. The problem is scale: computing those gradients for large models is very expensive.

Popular shortcuts use random projection to shrink the gradient data. The team's 2026 preprint proposes LoRIF, which uses low-rank influence functions to keep attribution scalable. Knowing which examples drive a prediction helps teams find mislabeled data, trace strange outputs, and credit data sources. As models train on ever larger collections, attribution that cannot scale simply cannot be used.
arxiv-2601-22029:
Zhengyan Huan and co-authors introduce a new statistical problem they call the Ensemble Inverse Problem. Inverse problems work backward from effects to causes. Here the goal is not one hidden state but a whole ensemble. A population of possibilities, distributed according to a prior pushed forward through a known process.

Recovering the full distribution matters when uncertainty itself is the answer, as in forecasting, imaging, and simulation-based science. Their 2026 preprint defines the problem and develops methods for it, with applications in view. Framing ensemble inversion cleanly could unify tricks now scattered across fields, from weather prediction to medical imaging. Where ensembles are already the working language of uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-22229:
Philip Hopkins and four co-authors ask if fast particles can fake the look of a cool core in a galaxy cluster. Cool cores are dense, bright hubs where gas has had time to cool. Their 2026 preprint notes that these hubs hold strong sources that speed up cosmic rays.

Some rays fade fast, but a long-lived pool of slower rays remains. When those rays hit gas, they can add glow that looks like fresh cooling. The team weigh how much this glow could skew what telescopes report. Their work warns that core heat reads may need a second look.
arxiv-2601-22329:
Ala Tak and a large team ask whether reasoning models judge like people do. Their 2026 preprint notes that models now help with hiring, health, and money choices. Real human judgment mixes clear thought with feeling-driven bias. A model used as a stand-in should mirror that mix, or the gap should be known.

The team probe where model choices match human ones, and where they part ways. They look for signs of the same quirks and blind spots. The work helps teams decide when a model's judgment can be trusted. It also warns where it cannot.
arxiv-2601-22429:
Weijia Chen and Jingtao Shi study a leader-and-crowd game where chance rules each move. One leader acts first; a vast crowd of followers react, each tied to the rest by a graphon, a limit shape for large networks. Their 2026 preprint uses linear-quadratic costs, the classic tractable form for such games.

The followers' states link through the graphon, and noise terms hinge on state and control too. The math seeks the best play for leader and crowd alike. Such games model grids, markets, and fleets at scale. The work extends game theory to huge, linked crowds.
arxiv-2601-22529:
Seung Hyun Lee, Sangwoo Mo, and Stella Yu built SHED, a model that reads every pixel of an image while honoring scene structure. Dense prediction, as this task is called, feeds 3D sensing and robotics. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools treat each pixel alone, which yields ragged, clashing maps.

SHED bakes a geometric prior — a built-in sense of shape — into its encoder-decoder frame. The result should be maps that hang together as real scenes do. Cleaner maps help robots move and grasp with trust. The work is a design fix for a core vision task.
arxiv-2601-22629:
Jingxuan Wu and a large team coax more variety from diffusion language models with a timed noise trick. Diffusion models build text by cleaning noise; for language, that path can yield samey outputs. Their 2026 preprint uses time-annealed perturbation sampling: noise added on a schedule that fades as the text firms up.

Early noise opens many paths; late calm locks a clean result. More variety, at no quality cost, helps drafting and brainstorming tools. The method is a sampling tweak, not a new model. That makes it cheap to adopt. The work targets a known dullness.
arxiv-2601-22829:
Marco Ghimenti, Anna Maria Micheletti, and Angela Pistoia study the tones, or eigenvalues, of elliptic problems on bounded regions. Their problems mix two kinds of boundary rules, named Steklov and Robin. The main question is whether the tones are all distinct, with no repeats.

For a typical region shape, the authors prove every eigenvalue is simple, meaning it occurs just once. They reach this by nudging the region's shape and checking how the operators respond. Distinct tones simplify the math of vibration, heat flow, and related physical systems. Simple eigenvalues also make numerical computation cleaner, since each tone can be tracked without confusion from repeated values.
arxiv-2601-22929:
Yiyi Chen and four co-authors show that image embeddings can leak more meaning than expected. Embeddings compress an image into numbers for search and tagging, and are often treated as low-risk to share. The authors define semantic leakage as the recovery of meaning structures from those compressed numbers.

They show such leakage does not need the original image to be rebuilt. Even rough recovery can reveal what a photo shows, and that is a privacy concern. Services that share embeddings for photos should treat them as sensitive data.
arxiv-2601-23029:
Gábor Szabó proves a general uniqueness theorem for Kasparov theory, a tool in operator algebra. The result answers a question raised by Carrión and co-authors in a landmark paper on classifying C-star algebras. Uniqueness theorems say when two constructions must give the same answer.

Given two separable algebras and a pair of absorbing representations, the induced KK-theory element vanishes under the stated conditions. Such vanishing results are the engine behind classification programs for algebras. They tell mathematicians when deep structural questions have a single possible answer.
arxiv-2601-23129:
Yilun Hua and four co-authors measure whether retrieved documents actually help a language model answer. Retrieval augmented generation lives or dies by the utility of its grounding content. Existing utility metrics ignore what a given model can use, or need costly human labels.

Their metric, GroGU, is model-specific and needs no reference answers. It scores utility from the model's own generation confidence, based on entropy. Cheap, tailored scoring could help systems fetch documents that truly improve answers. Generation confidence, measured through entropy, ties the utility score to the specific downstream model being served.
arxiv-2601-23229:
Ali Asadi and five co-authors bound the running time of policy looping for robust decision problems. Markov decision problems model sequential choices under doubt. Robust versions allow transition probabilities to vary within a set, and optimize against the worst case in that set.

For the L-infinity doubt model studied, they prove policy looping runs in strongly polynomial time. The model is expressive, covering classical problems and stochastic games. A firm time bound tells planners the method will finish predictably, not just eventually. Strongly polynomial bounds are the strong form of guarantee, independent of the numerical size of the inputs.

berkman-abc-anarchism-1929:
Alexander Berkman published The ABC of Anarchism in 1929, first issued as Now and After: The ABC of Communist Anarchism by Vanguard Press. Late in life, Berkman set out to state his creed in the plainest words he could find. Stuart Christie later praised it among the best such guides in English.

In question-and-answer form, Berkman asked why workers are poor amid plenty and what a free society would do instead. He attacked wages, bosses, and the state, and sketched shared work and free agreement in their place. No jargon blocks the way. The book still serves as a first door into anarchist thought for new readers.
bernard-guide-to-grand-jury-men-english-:
Richard Bernard, a Puritan minister, wrote A Guide to Grand-Jury Men in 1629. The two books instruct jurors who must decide whether accused witches go to trial. Bernard sets out how to spot witchcraft, weigh confessions, and judge evidence, step by step.

His guide became the standard English clerical handbook for witch-finding. Bernard urges care in places, yet the system he builds points toward conviction. Reading it now is chilling in a quiet way. The persecution here has an instruction book, coolly written by a man of God. Few texts show better how law, theology, and fear worked together in a witch trial.
bernard-light-on-masonry-1829:
David Bernard published Light on Masonry in 1829, at the height of anger against Freemasonry in the United States. Bernard had been a Mason, and he gathered oaths, rituals, and lodge papers to expose them. Anti-Masonic readers treated his book as their main source.

Inside are the words and signs of several Masonic degrees, along with charges, prayers, and accounts of lodge work. Bernard argued that secret oaths bound members in ways that clashed with law and faith. The book helped fuel a political movement, and it still shows what critics feared the lodge was doing behind closed doors.
black-sinanthropus-further-remains-1929:
Davidson Black reported further Peking Man fossils in Science in 1929. Excavations at Choukoutien, near Peking, kept yielding jaws and teeth. The growing sample belonged to the form he called Sinanthropus pekinensis.

Black stresses a curious mix in the fossils. The teeth look human while the jaw keeps an ape-like shape. That combination strengthened the case that Peking Man was truly an early human. The finds are now grouped with Homo erectus. Black's paper records the discovery phase, just before the first complete skullcap made headlines worldwide. Work at the cave continued through the following decade with growing success.
boguet-examen-of-witches-1929:
Henry Boguet judges witches in An Examen of Witches, here in the English text of 1929. Boguet was a judge in Burgundy whose bench saw scores of witch trials round 1600. His French book of 1602 is set here by Ashwin, with notes by Montague Summers. It lays out the sabbath, the pact, and the mark. It gives the rules of proof a judge should use at trial.

He prints cases from his own court in grim rows. His calm makes the book more dread than wild tracts. It is the hunt's hand book by a chief hand.
burns-introducing-bc-hairy-giants-1929:
John Burns gave the hairy giants of British Columbia their famed name in print in 1929. Introducing B C's Hairy Giants appeared in Maclean's Magazine that April. Burns was a teacher and agent among the Chehalis people, whose tales he set down with care.

From their word Sasq'ets he shaped Sasquatch, the name the wild men carry to this day. His article gathers the old tales and fresh reports of the great hairy tribe. With it, the modern Bigfoot era can be said to start in earnest. Few magazine pieces have named a legend so well.
butler-fifteen-sermons-1729:
Joseph Butler preached his Fifteen Sermons at the Rolls Chapel in London, and they were published in 1729 with his preface. The Rolls Chapel served the lawyers of the nearby courts, and Butler spoke to sharp, worldly hearers. His subject is human nature itself: how self-love, benevolence, and conscience fit together in one soul.

Butler argues that conscience, cool and reflective, holds the top place in our design by nature. Self-love and kindness to others, rightly read, never truly clash. The sermons founded his moral psychology and quietly changed English ethics. Philosophers still assign the sermon on conscience and the ones on self-deception. All fifteen stand here, the ground floor of Butler's fame.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-1-192:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk of the Rhineland, wrote his Dialogue on Miracles around 1219 to 1223 as a teaching book for novices. H. von E. Scott and C. C. Swinton Bland translated it into English in 1929, and this is the first volume. The dialogue form lets a monk ask and a master answer with tale after tale.

The stories run from conversion and confession to demons, visions, and the punishments of the wicked dead. Cathars appear at first hand, for Caesarius had ridden with the Albigensian Crusade's preachers. His exempla were preached across Europe for centuries. The book is the great medieval story chest of the miraculous, told with a gossip's glee and a monk's moral.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-2-192:
The second volume of the Scott and Bland English Caesarius, from 1929, completes the Dialogue on Miracles. Caesarius of Heisterbach wrote the work around 1219 to 1223 to stock Cistercian novices with tales for the road of the spirit. A full index closes the translation.

Temptations, visions of heaven and hell, and the deaths of saints and sinners fill these books. The Virgin Mary steps in again and again to save her servants, sometimes by rough mercy. Caesarius collected his tales from monks, knights, and travelers, and he names his sources. The dialogue between the questioning novice and the answering monk keeps the pace light. It is the middle ages talking to itself about wonder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-confe: This 1913 reference piece on the English confessors and martyrs — 1534 to 1729. John Hungerford Pollen honors the glorious roll. The priests died on the scaffold. The laymen shared the martyr's crown. The saints of the penal centuries. Their 1987 beatifications are famed.
charron-of-wisdom-stanhope-1729:
Pierre Charron, a French priest and the friend of Montaigne, published De la Sagesse, Of Wisdom, in 1601. George Stanhope's English translation, in the three-volume form of 1729, is the text here. All three books stand complete: self-knowledge first, then the wise man's conduct in life and in every station.

Charron builds his wisdom on honest doubt: know yourself, hold your judgments loosely, and let nature and reason lead. His skepticism, learned from Montaigne's Essays, aims not at despair but at calm freedom of mind. The book was attacked as godless and read everywhere in secret and in open. It carried Montaigne's spirit into the next century's philosophy.

A witness from the captors' own side offered rare inside detail. What was asked, and how, told analysts what the enemy wanted from prisoners. Deleted passages hide the source, as usual, but the account's core survives. The file shows testimony crossing enemy lines, with the censor's black marks still plainly on it.
cia-0000012429:
One redacted person debriefs another in a CIA record from February 1962, and both names stay blacked out. The record belongs to the Penkovsky era's questioning, the daily work of drawing knowledge out of people. Each of them had seen some piece of the puzzle the service was assembling. The debriefer's art shows in the answers: what they reveal, and what they leave carefully unsaid.

Such sessions filled the spaces between the great meetings in London and Paris. They tested stories, dated memories, and priced the rumors that reached the station. For readers, the page shows the interrogation rooms' quiet craft, where the big case was checked.
cia-0000013229:

That office set the rules for handling prisoners across the south. In plain terms, he was one of the prison system's administrators. His sections and signatures shaped what happened to men held in camps he may never have visited in person.

The item profiles the jailer's career and his place in the machine. Naming the jailers was the accounting's necessary, sobering work. For readers, the page puts a human face on a system too often described without one.

A National Intelligence Analytical Memorandum dated February 1, 1977 takes up the Ethiopian revolution and its impact. Ethiopia's emperor had been overthrown in 1974, and a military regime held power. The Horn of Africa was becoming a new Cold War battleground.

Inside, analysts weigh what the revolution meant for Ethiopia and its neighbors. They judge the new regime's direction and the openings it gave outside powers. Ethiopia's size and place made its turn matter far beyond its borders. The file captures a turning point in the region. An ancient empire became a Marxist state. The superpowers then recalculated their positions along the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
cia-0000042129:

Inside, the record marks a court step: the trial of the accused would go ahead. Getting soldiers into a courtroom was itself a hard fight in that war. The file shows the case moving, slowly, through a legal system under strain. It stands as one dated point in a long effort to make the killings answerable in court.
cia-0000042829:

Inside, the general gives his account in question and answer form. Senior officers rarely faced the press at such a moment. His words were read, in San Salvador and in Washington, for what they admitted and for what they carefully avoided saying aloud. The file preserves a commander defending his institution in public, while some of its members sat accused of the war's most famous murders.

Inside, the president's frank admission is preserved as he made it. Candor of that kind can steady a public or alarm it further. In a father's mouth, it sounded less like policy than like grief. The file keeps the remark from that September day. The most powerful man in the country told reporters, in effect, that he was waiting like everyone else.
