Yards serving the south stood nearly bare, while lines to the east ran four to eight tracks and bustled. Warehouses along the Spree were packed with machine tools, motors, and printing presses awaiting shipment. Work crews in Russian uniform loaded flat cars around the clock. Crating advanced visibly in a single day between the two visits.
gao-gaoreports-b-296029: Poly-Pacific Technologies took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299929: A second 2007 GAO ruling for AlliedBarton Security Services LLC — three more contract fights, same year, same firm. The guard company kept challenging federal awards, and GAO kept the calls coming. Read with its twin ruling, the pair maps how the government buys guard work — and how hard the big firms fight for it.
gao-gaoreports-b-304829: James Guckert's press release reprinting got a fiscal ruling in this June 2005 GAO call, which tests the reprinting. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the practice was legal. The law had the final word. The practice had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-307529: The Capitol Police's erroneous salary payments got a waiver ruling in this March 2006 GAO call, which tests forgiving the overpayments. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the mistaken paychecks could be forgiven. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310329: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Blane International Group, Inc. The December 13, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-311329: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Alliance Technical Services, Inc. Decided May 30, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-229: GSA contract pricing needed sharpening in 2005, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to improve the schedule prices. The review haggles for the taxpayer. The government's shopping list deserved the better deals. The pricing had to improve. The government's shopping list deserved the better deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-329: The bomb-securing program's books got better in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon's money controls improved, though woes stayed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the bomb-securing work deserved finishing. The bomb-securing work deserved finishing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-429: VA buildings had to fit the mission in 2005, and GAO's report says matching bricks to care was the hard part. The findings demand the fit. The report warns that the veterans deserved well-placed hospitals. The veterans deserved well-placed hospitals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-829: The Great Lakes water standards needed consistent implementation in 2005, and GAO's report says EPA had to ensure complete and uniform application. The findings demand the consistency. The report warns that the lakes deserved clean water. The implementation had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-929: Boutique doctors got a GAO look in 2005, and the report sizes up the pay-up-front practice and its Medicare angles. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the retainer doctors deserved scrutiny. The retainer doctors deserved scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1029: Nuclear plant oversight was improving in 2006, and GAO's report says the regulator's watch had gotten better, though refinements were needed. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the reactors deserved relentless vigilance. The watch could not blink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-429: The pension backstop's books needed daylight in 2006, and GAO's report says the reporting could be clearer. The findings target the fog. The report warns that the retirees' safety net deserved open books. The books had to be open. The safety net deserved clear books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-629: Geothermal energy faced hurdles in 2006, and GAO's report says increased development would depend on overcoming many challenges. The findings map the obstacles. The report warns that the earth's heat was free but hard to tap. The challenges had to be overcome.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-829: America's overseas footprint needed consolidating in 2006, and GAO's report says State and USAID should adopt a comprehensive support plan. The findings demand the blueprint. The report warns that the scattered outposts needed joining up. The presence had to be efficient.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-929: Credit card fine print was getting trickier in 2006, and GAO's report says the growing complexity heightened the need for clearer disclosures. The findings demand the plain talk. The report warns that the plastic's traps needed sunlight. The disclosures had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1129: A reactor-building boom was brewing in 2007, and GAO checked whether the atom referees were ready. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's licensing gears and staffing mostly passed, GAO found — but big unknowns hung over the coming flood of plant bids. The report tests the safety watchdog on the eve of its busiest stretch in decades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-29: Credit unions needed more sunlight in 2007, and GAO's report says transparency was lacking on who they served and what bosses earned. The findings demand the disclosure. The report warns that the member-owned banks should act like it. The books had to open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-629: The IRS's own audit report card came due in 2007 — GAO's letter tracks the financial audit and the fixes still owed. The findings keep the tax agency's books under a watchful eye. The letter's premise: the collector must itself be beyond reproach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-729: Foreign airports got American report cards in 2007 — GAO's report says overseas assessments and carrier inspections lifted security, but the watch needed work. The findings balance credit and caution. The report's reach: the sky has no borders, so neither should the screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-29: Published in 2007 by the Government Accountability Office, this report examines safety on airport runways and ramp areas. It reviews leadership gaps, technology shortfalls, and other challenges that contribute to accidents and near-misses where aircraft operate on the ground. The report calls for sustained effort across agencies to reduce runway incursions and ground collisions, and it grades the federal response to a long-standing aviation safety problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-529: The Government Accountability Office dug into medicaid Home and Community-Based Waivers: CMS Should Encourage States to Conduct Mortality Reviews for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
givry-musee-des-sorciers-1929:
Émile-Jules Grillot de Givry published Le Musée des sorciers, mages et alchimistes in French in 1929. The title calls the book a museum of sorcerers, mages, and alchemists, and the word museum fits. Givry gathered images and records the way a keeper gathers objects for display.

The result is a visual and written history of the grimoire tradition, the spell books passed down from the Middle Ages. Plates and documents fill the pages alongside Givry's accounts of the men who made and used them. The survey runs from medieval times toward the 1700s. Few single books show the look of the old magic world so fully.
guazzo-compendium-maleficarum-1929:
Francesco Maria Guazzo, a Milanese friar, first published the Compendium Maleficarum in 1608 as a handbook on witchcraft. The English text here is Montague Summers's translation of 1929. Guazzo gathered what courts and church writers of his day believed about witches, pacts with the Devil, and how such crimes should be proved and punished.

Pages sort witches into kinds, describe night gatherings and harmful spells, and list signs judges might use at trial. Cures, prayers, and exorcism close the work. Few books show the logic of the witch trials so fully, which makes it grim but key reading for that era of fear.
hegel-science-logic-johnston-vol-1-1929:
G. W. F. Hegel published his Science of Logic between 1812 and 1816, his most rigorous work. Volume 1 appears here in the 1929 translation by W. H. Johnston and L. G. Struthers. The Logic studies pure thought itself, starting from being and nothing. Categories unfold by dialectic, each giving rise to the next.

Volume 1 covers the Doctrine of Being and the start of the Doctrine of Essence. Quality, quantity, and measure receive long and careful treatment. Hegel meant the work to replace the formal logic of his day. Later dialectical theories all answer to it in some way. It is the hardest core of his system.
hegel-science-logic-johnston-vol-2-1929:
G. W. F. Hegel's Science of Logic reaches completion in Volume 2, given here in the same 1929 translation. This volume finishes the Doctrine of Essence and adds the Doctrine of the Notion. Essence deals with ground, appearance, and actuality. The Notion deals with concepts, judgments, and the Idea itself.

Hegel argues that logic and reality share one deep structure. Thought, fully developed, arrives at the Absolute Idea. The prose is abstract to a degree few books match. Readers need patience and, ideally, help from guides. With Volume 1, the work states his system in its purest form. Philosophers still wrestle with its claims.
heindel-rosicrucian-cosmo-conception-192:
Max Heindel founded the American Rosicrucian movement on the scheme set out in The Rosicrucian Cosmo-Conception. First printed in 1909, the book is given here in its 1929 form. Heindel called his teaching mystic Christianity, a path of growth for the soul.

He maps the worlds seen and unseen, man's bodies, death, rebirth, and the long road of the spirit. Christ stands at the center of his scheme as the guide of the coming age. The book trains the student in a full system, step by step. It remains the founding text of Heindel's fellowship to this day.
hemingway-farewell-to-arms-1929:
Ernest Hemingway published A Farewell to Arms in 1929, his novel of the Italian front. An ambulance driver's desertion and doomed love with a British nurse give the war novel's classic its human center. Hemingway had served and been wounded on that front, and the book burns with firsthand knowledge of its world.

Frederic Henry, an American in Italy's ambulance service, loves Catherine Barkley, a nurse, amid hospitals and mountain drives in wartime. The Caporetto retreat, rendered in famous plain prose, scatters the army and nearly costs Henry his life by firing squad. He deserts, rows to Switzerland with Catherine, and their idyll ends in a childbirth death in the rain. The close, he walks back to the hotel in the rain, is American prose's most imitated shrug at fate. Its anti-war feeling and spare style fixed Hemingway's world reputation.
hubble-distance-radial-velocity-1929:
Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer at Mount Wilson, published this short paper in 1929. He had already shown that fuzzy 'nebulae' are in fact galaxies far beyond our own. Now he compared their distances with the speeds at which they move away.

Hubble found a clear pattern: the farther a galaxy sits, the faster it recedes. That simple rule, now called Hubble's law, meant the universe is expanding. It gave Lemaître's theory hard proof from the sky. Modern measures of the age and size of the cosmos all start from this page. The paper is brief, but its graph changed astronomy for good.
husserl-formale-und-transzendentale-logi:
Edmund Husserl published Formal and Transcendental Logic in German in 1929. Husserl, teaching at Freiburg, had founded phenomenology, the study of how things appear to consciousness. Late in his career he returned to a question that had driven him from the start: what grounds logic itself?

The book distinguishes formal logic, the theory of consistent statements, from the deeper inquiry into how meaning arises in the mind that uses it. Husserl argues that logic cannot rest on symbols alone; it must be traced back to the acts of judgment that give symbols sense. The argument is dense and exacting, the capstone of a lifetime's thought. Scholars read it as phenomenology's mature statement on the foundations of reason, with meaning itself put under the microscope.
jeans-universe-around-us-1929:
James Jeans published The Universe Around Us in 1929, a popular account of modern astronomy. Jeans was a noted physicist and astronomer with a gift for clear prose. The book surveys the solar system, stars, nebulae, and the expanding universe. New findings on the size and age of the cosmos fill its pages.

Jeans writes for readers with no training in mathematics. He explains how light and spectra reveal the lives of stars. The final chapters ask what the new cosmos means for human life. The book sold science to millions in Britain and America. It helped define popular cosmology between the wars.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-29:
Antoine Daniel dies at St. Joseph in Volume 29, from 1898. Thwaites covers Iroquois attacks and French lands across 1647 and 1648 here. The great Iroquois assault on Huronia begins in earnest in these years.

Survivors record Daniel's death while the event is still fresh and raw. He stayed with his flock as the town burned around him. More attacks follow, and the reports read like a passion story. Grief and faith share the page as town after town falls to attack. The end of a world is near, and all can feel it. The mission's long Calvary opens in this grim, moving volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messiah-hebr-ha:
Messiah, from the Hebrew Ha-Mashiaḥ, meaning the anointed one, is the name for the ideal king of the Messianic age. Joseph Jacobs and Moses Buttenwieser wrote the long Jewish Encyclopedia article on the subject in 1906. It follows the word and the idea from the Old Testament through the prophets and into later Jewish writing.

The article shows that in the Bible the title first belongs to reigning kings and anointed priests, and even to Cyrus of Persia. Isaiah gives the fullest early picture: a scion of Jesse who rules in righteousness and brings peace, not war. Later sections treat Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the servant songs of Deutero-Isaiah, the Apocrypha, and Alexander the Great hailed as a deliverer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milcah-10829:
Milcah is a two-part name entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn. It sorts out two different women of the Bible who share the name. Neither gets a story of her own here; the entry is a signpost built from three verses of Genesis and one of Numbers.

The first Milcah, daughter of Haran, married her uncle Nahor and bore eight sons, the youngest being Bethuel, father of Rebekah. Ibn Ezra, the entry notes, doubted the uncle marriage, arguing her father was a different Haran from Abraham's brother. The second Milcah is simply listed as the fourth daughter of Zelophehad, with her sisters, in the census of Numbers.
kittredge-witchcraft-old-new-england-192:
George Lyman Kittredge was a Harvard man of great weight in his field. His Witchcraft in Old and New England came out in 1929. The book sweeps the trials of both Englands over three hundred years. It is the chief grave study of its theme in English.

Kittredge holds that belief in witchcraft was the norm, not a craze of fools. He works from court rolls, tracts, and tales of the day. Salem takes its place in a long, wide tale, not as a lone blot. The book still rules the study of Anglo witchcraft in the past.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-1:
Nathaniel Bowditch translated Laplace's Mecanique Celeste into English, with volume one reaching print in 1829. Laplace, often called the Newton of France, had summed up the math of the heavens. Books one and two cover balance, motion, and universal gravitation. Bowditch filled the margins with his own famed commentary.

His notes explain hard steps and correct or extend the French text. The translation taught American readers celestial mechanics at the highest level. It also made Bowditch's name as a scholar in two fields. Volume one begins a four volume set. The scale of the project still impresses. Patient readers gain a master class.
larsen-passing-1929:
Nella Larsen published Passing in 1929, a short novel about two childhood friends who meet again as adults. Irene Redfield lives as a Black woman in Harlem with her husband and sons. Clare Kendry passes as white and has married a racist white man. Their renewed friendship brings risk to both homes.

Clare longs for the Black world she left behind. Irene fears Clare's secret and her pull on Irene's husband. Tension builds toward a shocking final scene at a party. Larsen leaves key questions open for the reader to judge. The novel is a classic study of race, identity, and danger in America.
lenin-what-is-to-be-done-1929:
Lenin published What Is to Be Done in 1902, and it founded the Bolshevik idea of the party. The text here is the 1929 International Publishers version, from the Little Lenin Library. Russian socialists were split over how to organize against the tsar. Lenin answers with a call for a vanguard party of trained revolutionaries.

Workers alone, he argues, reach only trade union demands, not full socialist consciousness. A tight, disciplined party must bring that consciousness from outside. His attack on freedom of criticism as a slogan runs through the book. The argument shaped communist parties across the world. It remains Lenin's most debated early work.
lewis-dodsworth-1929:
Sinclair Lewis published Dodsworth in 1929, the mature masterpiece of his middle period. Lewis set it in Zenith and then across Europe, where he had been living part of each year. He wrote Sam Dodsworth with more sympathy than any hero since his earliest work.

Sam, a blunt automobile manufacturer, retires and takes his wife Fran on the European tour she craves. Fran, terrified of aging, hunts youth and aristocratic flirtation from London to Berlin. Sam, at first lost among the ruins and manners, slowly finds his own second life. The marriage comes apart in scenes of unusual fairness to both sides. Many readers now rank Dodsworth as Lewis's finest novel.
lewis-mind-world-order-1929:
Mind and the World Order, published in 1929, is C. I. Lewis's outline of a theory of knowledge, the book that founded conceptual pragmatism. Lewis, a Harvard philosopher, asks how the mind's own concepts shape the world it claims merely to find.

His answer: the a priori is pragmatic, made rather than found. Concepts are made by us, chosen for their use, yet once chosen they bind experience without exception. Knowledge is the reading of the given through such schemes. The argument joins Kant to Peirce in an original synthesis. The book influenced a generation of American philosophers and logicians.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-3-1929:
Book Three of Nicholson's Mathnawi came out in 1929. R. A. Nicholson gave Rumi's vast poem a full English dress with the Persian text. This book holds Books Five and Six of the poem. With it, the tale part of his set is done.

Rumi's tales grow more deep and wild as the poem nears its close. Love of God burns through tales of beasts, kings, and poor dervishes. The poem breaks off at the end, cut short by Rumi's death. Nicholson's notes clear the dense web of Sufi signs for the reader.
mckay-banjo-1929:
Claude McKay, the Jamaican-born poet of the Harlem Renaissance, published Banjo in 1929. McKay had wandered through America, London, and Soviet Russia before settling for a time in Marseille. He set the novel on that city's rough waterfront, among sailors and drifters from every shore.

The hero, Banjo, leads a loose band of Black seamen who play music, dodge work, and argue about race and art. His friend Ray, a Haitian writer, gives the talk a serious edge. Little plot holds the scenes together; the pleasure is in the talk, the music, and the port's mixed life. Banjo became a key novel of the Black Atlantic, read across three continents.
mo-tzu-mei-1929:
Yi-Pao Mei translated the works of Mo Tzu into English in 1929 as The Ethical and Political Works of Motse. The Mozi is the founding book of Mohism, the school that rivaled Confucianism in ancient China. Mo Tzu, who lived after Confucius, taught universal love in place of love graded by kinship.

The works attack wasteful funerals, aggressive war, and belief in blind fate. They prize merit in office, plain living, and proof by benefit to the people. Mei's version, in the Arthur Probsthain Oriental Series, was the first complete English Mozi. Mohism later faded in China, which makes the book doubly precious. It preserves a whole school of thought in its founder's own terms.
murad-the-unlucky-and-other-tales-pg2129: Maria Edgeworth's tales for the young, led by "Murad the Unlucky," an Eastern story of fortune and character. Moral, entertaining, and beautifully told, they taught generations. Classic children's literature from a master. Edgeworth's morals are gentle and her storytelling first-rate.
newton-principia-motte-1729:
Isaac Newton's Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy appeared in English in 1729, in Andrew Motte's translation. The Latin Principia of 1687 had set out Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation. Motte's version was the first in English, and it carried Newton to readers without Latin.

Newton showed that one law of gravity governs falling apples, the Moon, and the planets alike. He derived the paths of comets, the tides, and the shape of the Earth from a few stated laws. The math is hard, and Motte kept it close and plain. This translation shaped how the English-speaking world learned the founding work of modern physics.
objections-to-phrenology-being-the-subst: Objections to Phrenology, 1829. The anti-phrenology papers. The archive keeps it. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
observations-on-the-phrenological-develo: Observations on the Phrenological Development of Burke, Hare, 1829. The murderers' skulls. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
openalex-w1493890929: Crops were domesticated — but what happened to their root microbes? A 2015 review examines how plant domestication shaped the rhizosphere microbiome — the root-zone microbes — and its functions. The review asked whether breeding weakened the microbe partnerships that protect crops.
openalex-w2008789929: Brazil slashed malaria from six million cases to hundreds of thousands. Oliveira-Ferreira and colleagues' 2010 overview traces malaria in Brazil — from ~6 million yearly cases in the 1940s to about 306,000 registered in 2009. The review surveyed the fight's history and remaining gaps.
openalex-w2019183229: Life needs nitrogen — even in the sunless deep. This work studied aphotic nitrogen fixation in the eastern tropical South Pacific. The thin catalog record hides the details, but the study probed how microbes fix nitrogen far below the light.
openalex-w2022091129: Plastic on the ocean surface is only half the story. Reisser and colleagues' 2015 observational study mapped the vertical distribution of buoyant plastics in the North Atlantic Gyre. The work showed turbulence mixes millimeter-sized plastics down through the water column.
openalex-w2081693829: Water plants build underwater neighborhoods. A 2010 review covers the role of water plants in shaping aquatic habitats. The work surveyed measuring methods, causes, and effects on animal communities — from bugs to waterbirds and fish alike.
openalex-w2127392229: Forests degrade — defining it is half the battle. A 2013 paper set out a working framework for defining and monitoring forest degradation. The framework gave managers a definition and monitoring tools — degradation, tamed at last for the field today and now.
openalex-w2128328029: Ultrasound could replace X-rays for pneumonia. A 2014 review pooled studies of lung ultrasound for spotting pneumonia in adults. The combined data weighed ultrasound against chest X-ray and CT — imaging's new hope, judged at last for clinicians now — bedside imaging's rise.
openalex-w2342951529: Each lead-lead collision at the LHC is a unique explosion, and the ripples in its debris — flow harmonics — fluctuate from event to event. This 2016 Physical Review Letters paper measures, for the first time, how those fluctuations correlate with each other, using a new multiparticle method. The correlations probe the lumpy initial geometry of the quark-gluon plasma and how it evolves.
openalex-w2921574129: A newborn's first week is a biological whirlwind — and systems biology is finally watching it closely. This 2019 Nature Communications paper tracks transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and immune changes through the first seven days of life. The molecular choreography follows a robust developmental trajectory, even in babies highly vulnerable to disease.
openalex-w2952946229: How a virus diversifies inside one host can decide the infection's outcome — but measuring it is hard. This 2019 Genome Biology paper evaluates PrimalSeq, a multiplexed amplicon approach, with the iVar framework, testing how virus concentration, coverage, primer mismatches, and replicates affect accuracy. The toolkit sharpens our view of within-host evolution.
openalex-w3009916829: Smallholder land-use changes can lift livelihoods — but at what ecological cost? This 2020 Nature Communications interdisciplinary study examines trade-offs between multifunctionality and profit in tropical smallholder landscapes. The analysis weighs the environmental, social, and economic consequences together.
openalex-w4392095629: Highly pathogenic avian influenza has caused waves of infection for a century — but the 2020–2023 panzootic may be the most consequential yet. This 2024 Emerging Infectious Diseases paper reviews recent changes in mammal infection patterns with H5N1 worldwide. The analysis tracks a virus on the move.
openalex-w7119516229: Potassium ions drift through water in ways that matter for batteries and biology. This paper studies their diffusion with pulsed-field gradient NMR, a magnetic technique that tracks molecular motion. The authors tackle the method's limits for these fast ions. A physical-chemistry study of salt on the move.
openalex-w7204279629: Maps can be acts of resistance. This article tells how the riverside community of Curupere Grande in Para mapped its own territory through social cartography, recording land, livelihood, and memory. The authors describe the project born from a geotechnology course. A vivid account of a traditional community drawing its own lines.
openalex-w7204785729: Glass that turns blue light into ultraviolet could serve sensors and sterilizers. This paper reports praseodymium-doped silica glasses, melted while levitating, emitting strong UV under blue excitation. The authors pushed past normal doping limits. A photonics study of glass that upgrades light.
outlines-of-phrenology-being-also-a-manu: Outlines of Phrenology, 1829. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
plos-pbio-0020029:
Jeffrey H. Chuang and Hao Li analyzed mutation patterns in the human genome for PLOS Biology in 2004. The rate of harmless change is not even along our chromosomes. Some stretches gather changes fast, while others stay stable for long spans.

The authors asked whether genes in fast and slow zones do different jobs. They found that the mix of functions does shift with the local rate of change. That pattern helps separate real signals of selection from plain background noise. Anyone hunting disease genes or signs of evolution needs that baseline. The paper is a map of where change comes easily and where it does not.
plos-pbio-0020129:
Thomas Bartman, Emily C. Walsh, Kuo-Kuang Wen, and their team used zebrafish to study heart growth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Inside the young heart, cushions of tissue form at key spots. Those cushions later become valves and walls that split the heart into chambers.

The authors found that how well the heart muscle works early on shapes how the cushions form. Blood flow and squeezing force are thus part of the building plan, not just results of it. That insight helps explain some birth defects of the heart, where weak early function may warp later form. Zebrafish, with clear embryos and visible hearts, make such links easy to watch live.
plos-pbio-0020329:
Winfried Denk and Heinz Horstmann unveiled a microscopy method in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their serial block-face scanning electron microscope cuts a tissue sample slice by slice. After each cut, it images the fresh face at very fine scale, then stacks the images into a 3D view.

Older methods needed hand-cut sections that tear and misalign. Cutting inside the microscope keeps every slice in register. The result is a full 3D map of tissue structure down to tiny cell parts. Brain wiring studies gained the most, since tracing thin nerve fibers through tissue is just what the method does best. It became a standard tool in connectomics, the mapping of brain circuits.
plos-pbio-0020429:
Nina Tang Sherwood, Qi Sun, Mingshan Xue, and their team studied a fly protein needed for movement in PLOS Biology in 2004. Spastin cuts microtubules, the stiff rods that nerve cells use as tracks and supports. In humans, faulty spastin causes a disease that stiffens the legs over time.

In flies, the team found spastin shapes the microtubule networks at synapses, the junctions where nerves meet muscle. Without it, those networks fray and the flies move poorly. That ties a human disease gene to a clear cell job. A fly that mimics the fault gives labs a fast way to test what goes wrong and what might fix it.
plos-pone-0000029:
Helmy Rachman, Nayoung Kim, Timo Ulrichs, and co-authors studied how tuberculosis germs push immune cells toward death in a 2006 paper. Macrophages are the immune cells that swallow mycobacteria, and apoptosis is their orderly self-destruction. Whether an infected macrophage dies, and how, helps decide who wins the fight.

The team found a critical role for methylglyoxal and for AGE, the advanced glycation end products that build up in tissue. Both drive the macrophage apoptosis and activation that mycobacteria trigger. That names two chemicals as levers in the TB immune response. Levers matter: blocking or boosting them could one day help the body clear an infection that still kills over a million people a year.
plos-pone-0000129:
Sarah L. Clarke, Gareth J. Betts, Andrea Plant, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It concerns colorectal cancer patients and a special set of immune cells called regulatory T cells, marked by CD4, CD25, and FOXP3. These cells normally calm immune responses down.

The authors report that these regulatory cells suppress the immune attack against the tumor in these patients. That helps explain how cancers can grow in a body that has a working immune system. The finding is relevant to cancer immunotherapy, where lifting such brakes is a main strategy for freeing the immune system to fight.
plos-pone-0000229:
Elizabeth Cudilo, Hamda Al Naemi, Lihua Marmorstein, and colleagues published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its framing question is blunt: knockout mice, is it just genetics? The mice carried one faulty copy of the fibulin-4 gene. The authors test whether enriched housing, a more stimulating cage environment, changes how the genetic defect plays out.

Genes load the dice, but surroundings roll them. If housing conditions shift the outcome of a mutation, then mouse studies must report and control those conditions carefully. The paper is part of a wider reckoning in animal research: environment is a variable, not background noise.
plos-pone-0000329:
Heather M. Scobie, John M. Marlett, G. Jonah A. Rainey, and colleagues published this anthrax study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Anthrax toxin enters cells by forming a pore, and that step depends on acidity. The authors identify the determinants in anthrax toxin receptor 2 that dictate the pH threshold at which the pore forms. The receptor is one of the toxin's two doors into cells.

The pH threshold decides where inside the cell the toxin strikes. Pinpointing what sets it explains differences between the two receptors. The detail matters for anthrax defense research, where blocking the toxin's entry is a main strategy.
plos-pone-0000429:
Frank Röck and colleagues measured the chemicals in mouse urine to test how the immune system shapes scent, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mice can smell differences tied to the MHC, a set of immune genes that also varies between individuals. The team ran a quantitative analysis of urine volatiles, the airborne chemicals urine gives off, searching for MHC-dependent differences.

If immune genes reliably change body odor, scent becomes an honest signal of genetic difference, which mice may use when choosing mates. A careful chemical census is the groundwork for that claim: it shows which molecules actually differ. The work sits where immunology meets animal communication.
plos-pone-0000529:
Hidehiro Watanabe and Makoto Mizunami demonstrated textbook conditioning in a cockroach, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their paper, titled Pavlov's Cockroach, described classical conditioning of salivation in an insect. The cockroach learned to salivate at a cue that predicted food. Pavlov's dogs learned in much the same way.

Salivation is measurable and the insect brain is small, making the cockroach a tractable model for how associations form. Insect learning studies usually track movement or feeding choices; a salivary response gives a cleaner readout. The work supports the view that the basic machinery of associative learning is ancient and shared across very different animals.
plos-pone-0000629:
Chun Lai Nie, Yan Wei, Xinyong Chen and co-authors tested what low levels of formaldehyde do to the tau protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tau normally supports nerve cells, but misfolded, clumped tau is closely tied to neurodegeneration. The team's earlier work showed tau clumping in formaldehyde solution. Those clumps also drove cultured nerve-like and hippocampal cells toward apoptosis, programmed cell death.

Here they report that even low formaldehyde concentrations push tau into round, amyloid-like aggregates, both in vitro and in vivo. Formaldehyde is a common chemical in labs, industry, and the body itself. A link to tau clumping raises questions well beyond one experiment.
plos-pone-0000729:
Patrick Williamson, Margaret S. Halleck, Jonathan Malowitz and colleagues examined lipid movements in cells missing a key transporter, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Tangier disease is an inherited disorder leaving patients with very low levels of HDL, the so-called good cholesterol carrier. Mutations in the ABCA1 gene cause it. How faults in that ATP-driven transporter produce the outcome was not known.

The team studied transbilayer phospholipid movements, lipids flipping between the two layers of the cell membrane, in ABCA1-deficient cells. If the transporter normally flips lipids, its loss explains the HDL failure. Membrane asymmetry turns out to be maintained work, not a given, and Tangier disease shows the cost.
plos-pone-0000829:
Erika Tamm, Toomas Kivisild, Maere Reidla and colleagues reconstructed how the first Americans waited, then spread, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Native Americans derive from a small number of Asian founders who likely arrived via Beringia, the land bridge region between Siberia and Alaska. Details of that initial colonization remained unclear. To investigate the pioneering phase, the team analyzed a total of 623 mitochondrial samples.

Their title names the pattern: a Beringian standstill, then spread. The founders apparently paused in Beringia long enough to become genetically distinct before moving into the Americas. That pause, written in maternal lineages, reshapes the timeline of the peopling of two continents.
plos-pone-0000929:
Daniel Nettle, James Grace, Marc Choisy and colleagues tested whether cultural diversity makes nations unstable, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Social scientists had long suggested that many cultures within one nation breed unrest. The authors argue the picture is wider: diversity between a nation and its neighbors may matter as much as diversity inside it.

They also bring economic development into the test. Instability may track poverty more than culture. Sorting those forces apart matters for policy, since the fixes differ. The study treats a familiar claim as a question to be measured, not a fact to be repeated. Its care with definitions is part of the contribution.
plos-pone-0001029:
Elena Makareeva and Sergey Leikin studied how the collagen triple helix gets built despite preferring to unravel, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Type I collagen forms the scaffold of bone and many tissues. Oddly, at body temperature a lone collagen triple helix would rather be a random coil; only in fibers do neighbors hold it stable.

The authors describe an unconventional folding path assisted by chaperones, helper proteins. How the helix assembles before neighbors exist is the puzzle they address. The answer matters for diseases where collagen folds wrong, weakening bone and skin. It also refines basic protein folding ideas, since this helix breaks the usual rules.
plos-pone-0001129:
Early-stage lung cancer can be cured by surgery, yet patients at the same stage often fare very differently. Rafael Rosell and co-authors looked for a gene that helps explain that spread, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their candidate was BRCA1, a gene better known from breast and ovarian cancer.

The study covers non-small-cell lung cancer that was removed by surgery. Gene expression profiles can sort patients into groups with different outlooks even within one stage. The authors present BRCA1 as a new prognostic factor, meaning its levels carry information about likely survival. Such markers could one day guide who needs extra treatment after surgery.
plos-pone-0001229:
Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis causes chronic gut inflammation in many animals, including primates, and people encounter it through milk and the environment. Tim Bull and colleagues tested a new vaccine against it in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Existing vaccines against this bacterium were limited.

The authors describe a novel multi-antigen vaccine delivered by a viral vector, a harmless virus carrying several of the bacterium's proteins. Presenting multiple antigens at once may protect better than single-antigen designs. The work targets a livestock disease with possible, debated links to human Crohn's disease.
plos-pone-0001329:
Myxococcus xanthus is a bacterium with a social life: starved cells swarm together and build fruiting bodies, mounds that produce spores. Barry Goldman, Swapna Bhat, and Lawrence Shimkets traced how that ability evolved, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lateral gene transfer, the swapping of genes between bacteria, is thought to promote speciation, though well-defined examples were lacking.

The authors examined the evolutionary history of the genes essential for fruiting body development, a trait that defines a whole phylogenetic order of bacteria. Their genome analysis tests whether borrowed genes built this complex behavior. The study is a case history in bacterial innovation.
plos-pone-0001429:
Jeroen van Boxtel, David Alais, and Casper Erkelens published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on binocular rivalry, when each eye gets a unlike image. The brain flips between the two views, a play called binocular rivalry. The work probes how coarse form data shapes those flips. It bears on how the brain settles clashes and builds a single view.

The authors test whether rough, fast form cues set the pace of the flips. Their results give weight to a role for coarse form in early vision. That helps sort which brain stages solve the clash. The study adds to the science of how aware sight emerges from mixed signals.
plos-pone-0001529:
Niels Lynnerup and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on proteins in the eye lens. Lens proteins are sealed in at birth, with no blood flow or cell shed to renew them. That seal makes them a record of a whole life. The team used carbon dating to age these proteins in human lenses.

Their dates show the core lens proteins are as old as the person. No new carbon enters them through life. That makes the lens a birth date stamp that lasts to death. Forensic teams can use it to age unknown remains when other marks fail.
plos-pone-0001629:
Tanya Detto, Jan M. Hemmi, and Patricia R. Y. Backwell described the colors and color changes of a fiddler crab in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The species is Uca capricornis. Many animals change color in response to social or surroundings-based cues, and the change can take seconds or months. Crabs and their kin are known to be very good at this.

The study is descriptive: it records what colors this crab shows and how and when they shift. The full text gives the patterns the authors watched, the settings in which changes took place, and how this species compares with other fiddler crabs. Careful records like this form the base for later work on why crabs change color. The reasons may include signaling to rivals and mates, or hiding from hunters.
plos-pone-0001729:
Qiming Jin, Guobao Wei, Zhao Lin, and their co-authors built a scaffold that releases a wound-healing factor in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Platelet-derived growth factor, PDGF, stimulates repair in many tissues. Its clinical use is held back by delivery. The body clears it fast, so the release system controls how much reaches a wound and for how long.

The team loaded PDGF-BB into microspheres inside nanofibrous scaffolds. In living tissue, the scaffolds induced chemokine expression and new tissue growth, per the paper's title. The full text gives the scaffold design, the release rates, and the tissue results. Better delivery scaffolds could turn many lab-proven growth factors into practical wound treatments.
plos-pone-0001829:
Norman Warthmann, Hao Chen, Stephan Ossowski, and their co-authors engineered artificial microRNAs for rice in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Endogenous microRNAs are potent negative regulators of gene expression in plants and animals. Artificial miRNAs, designed to target chosen genes, provide a highly specific approach for post-transcriptional gene silencing.

The team reports highly specific gene silencing by artificial miRNAs in rice, with little off-target effect. The full text gives the design rules and the silencing measurements. Rice feeds half the world. A precise gene-off switch helps researchers test gene functions and helps breeders fine-tune traits without foreign DNA in the final plant.
plos-pone-0001929:
Lincoln Shenje and co-authors traced the roots of cells grown from heart tissue, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When bits of heart are grown in a dish, they yield a mixed crop of cells. Among them sits a distinct group of small round cells, which the team calls cardiac explant derived cells.

The group used lineage tracing, a way to mark a cell's source and follow its offspring, to find where these round cells come from. They also charted the cells' shape and their power to become heart cells. If such cells can make new heart muscle, they could one day help repair hearts after damage.
plos-pone-0002029:
Sung-Kook Hong, Michael Tsang, and Igor Dawid studied a growth gene in the zebrafish embryo, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The neural crest is a band of early cells that builds much of the face and other parts. One family member, c-Myc, was known to help set up the neural crest in frogs and to shape the face in mice.

What other Myc family genes do in the crest was unknown, as was any role for zebrafish Myc genes in growth. As the title states, the gene Mych is required for neural crest cells to survive in zebrafish. The find adds a life-or-death switch to crest biology.
plos-pone-0002129:
Tao Sun and co-authors used computer modeling to study how skin cells grow in the lab, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, are grown for medical use with help from mouse feeder cells and cow serum. Safety worries about these animal products have pushed labs to find cleaner ways to grow the cells.

The team built an agent-based model, a simulation where each cell follows simple rules and the group pattern emerges. Their model helped show the rules by which the feeder cells support colony growth. That insight can guide lab methods that drop the animal products while keeping the growth patients need.
plos-pone-0002229:
Patrick Leclerc and co-authors studied a partner protein of an inflammation enzyme in human white blood cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme COX-2 appears when tissues are inflamed and also plays roles in tumor growth and normal body function. Much about its biology was still open when the study began.

The team focused on nucleobindin, a widespread protein found in the same places as COX-2 inside neutrophils, the most common white blood cells. They show the two proteins associate with each other. A binding partner can reveal how COX-2 is controlled, which matters for pain and inflammation drugs that target it.
plos-pone-0002329:
Li Zeng and co-authors studied how saturated fats change a cell's answer to DNA damage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. DNA damage triggers signals that pause the cell cycle or order the cell to die, a response that guards against cancer. Fatty acid synthesis is raised in many human tumors, while blocking it can slow tumor growth.

The team reports that saturated fatty acids modulate the response to DNA damage. That modulation may help damaged cells survive when they should die, a step toward tumor formation. The link between dietary-style fat chemistry and the damage alarm adds one more route by which fat may feed cancer risk.
plos-pone-0002429:
Lindner and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Alberto Lindner, Stephen D. Cairns, Clifford W. Cunningham, among others. Its subject is from Offshore to Onshore: Multiple Origins of Shallow-Water Corals from Deep-Sea Ancestors. Shallow-water tropical reefs and the deep sea represent the two most diverse marine environments.

Understanding the origin and diversification of this biodiversity is a major quest in ecology and evolution. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002529:
Losin, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Elizabeth A. Reynolds Losin, Jamie L. Russell, Hani Freeman, among others. Its subject is left Hemisphere Specialization for Oro-Facial Movements of Learned Vocal Signals by Captive Chimpanzees. The left hemisphere of the human brain is dominant in the production of speech and signed language.

Whether similar lateralization of function for communicative signal production is present in other primates remains a topic of considerable debate. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002629:
In 2008, Daniela Paclik and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was galectin-4 controls intestinal inflammation by selective regulation of peripheral and mucosal t cell apoptosis and cell cycle. The catalog record names Daniela Paclik first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Galectin-4 is a carbohydrate-binding protein belonging to the galectin family. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002729:
In 2008, Marie-Florence Galliano and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was binding of α2ML1 to the low density lipoprotein Receptor-Related protein 1 (LRP1) reveals a new role for LRP1 in the human epidermis. Authorship is credited in the record to Marie-Florence Galliano and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The multifunctional receptor LRP1 has been shown to bind and internalize a large number of protein ligands with biological importance such as the pan-protease. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002829:
In 2008, Sung-Min Ahn and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about human microglial cells synthesize albumin in brain. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Sung-Min Ahn, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Albumin, an abundant plasma protein with multifunctional properties, is mainly synthesized in the liver. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002929:
Tsvetan Bachvaroff and Allen Place examined gene layout in the dinoflagellate Amphidinium carterae in 2008. Dinoflagellates are marine plankton with odd genomes: very large, with altered DNA bases, no nucleosomes, and tightly packed chromosomes. Many of their genes appear as numerous slightly different copies.

The PLOS ONE study covers tandem gene arrangement, copy number, and trans-splicing sites, the points where RNA pieces are joined. Together those features explain how these plankton organize a genome unlike most others. The work aids anyone sequencing or comparing dinoflagellate DNA, a group vital to ocean food webs. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003029:
Yuji Yoshiike, Tetsuya Kimura, Shunji Yamashita and co-authors linked GABA receptors to memory decline in Alzheimer's model mice in 2008. Advanced age and mutations in the APP and presenilin genes are two serious risk factors for Alzheimer's disease. Finding changes shared by both risks could suggest a new treatment strategy.

In APP/PS1 mice, GABA A receptor activity sped ageing-associated memory decline, and the drug picrotoxin treated that effect, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the lead is notable because boosting inhibition is usually expected to protect, not harm, memory. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003129:
Dennis M. Lindell, Aaron A. Berlin, Matthew A. Schaller and co-authors study B cells in long-term allergic lung disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The role of B cells in allergic asthma was still unclear. One clear route is their making of antibodies, above all IgE, and their close interaction with T cells, which in turn help B cells.

The title gives the main claim: when B cells present antigen, they promote Th2 responses and tissue damage during chronic allergic lung disease. Readers see why B cells matter beyond making IgE alone. The work may guide new ways to calm allergic asthma at its immune roots.
plos-pone-0003229:
Rebecca S. Mathew-Fenn and co-authors report a molecular ruler in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their ruler measures distances, and spreads of distances, inside big molecules, with a known scale for checks. They use X-ray scattering in solution, watching how two gold nanocrystal probes, fixed at set sites on a molecule, scatter in step.

Readers get a way to size the gaps in molecules as they float in fluid, not locked in crystals. A spread of distances shows flex that one still shape hides. Such rulers help test how proteins and RNA bend and shift as they work.
plos-pone-0003329:
Patrick M. Loerch, Tao Lu, Kelly A. Dakin and colleagues compare brain ageing across species in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders of ageing are characterized by clinical and pathological features relatively specific to humans. To obtain greater insight into how brain ageing has evolved, the team compared age-related gene expression changes in the cortex across species.

Their subject is evolution of the aging brain transcriptome and synaptic regulation. Readers learn which ageing changes are human-specific and which are shared. Shared changes point to core ageing biology, while human-specific ones may explain our particular vulnerability to dementia.
plos-pone-0003429:
Dario Alberto Dilernia and colleagues tracked HIV change across human groups in this 2008 study. Killer T cells force HIV to mutate around each person's immune fingerprint. Those fingerprints come from HLA genes, which vary between people. The team studied two HIV subtypes, B and F, at the population level.

Escape mutations in both subtypes pointed in like directions. Shared HLA pressure seemed to push the virus toward the same answers. That convergence matters for vaccine design across regions. If the virus dodges in set ways, vaccines can aim ahead of it.
plos-pone-0003529:
Rosa A. Cardone and co-authors traced a viral protein's chain of effects in this 2008 paper. Transformed cells share one trait: their insides turn more alkaline. A virus protein, HPV16 E7, pushes human cells toward cancer. Earlier work linked that transformation to a pump called NHE1.

The team mapped how E7 switches NHE1 on. The chain runs through PKA and RhoA, then blocks p38alpha. Each link tilts the cell's chemistry toward the cancer state. Knowing the chain names points where intervention might break it. HPV causes most cervical cancers, so its tricks draw close study.
plos-pone-0003629:
Karina Jin Yoon, Doris A. Phelps, Rebecca A. Bush, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It focuses on neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor, and a protein called ICAM-2. The team studied how ICAM-2 links the cell surface to the actin frame inside the cell.

Cells with ICAM-2 showed a form that did not spread, and tumors with it matched better stage or tissue type. The membrane-to-actin link seems to hold tumor cells in place. The authors present ICAM-2 as both a sign of a better outlook and a clue to how spread might be curbed.
plos-pone-0003729:
John Stover, Boga Fidzani, Batho Chris Molomo, and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Botswana has faced one of the world's most severe HIV epidemics. The team used surveillance, survey, and program data to estimate how the epidemic had moved over time.

They combined clinic records from antenatal care with a national population survey. From those sources they estimated past trends, current levels, and the effects of treatment and prevention programs. The report card shows what a hard-hit nation's response had achieved by 2008. Few countries had data this complete at the time.
plos-pone-0003829:
Sandeepa M. Eswarappa, Jessin Janice, Arvindhan G. Nagarajan, and colleagues published this Salmonella study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Salmonella enterica splits into many serovars that sicken birds and mammals. They differ greatly in host range, from narrow specialists to broad generalists. The basis of that specificity is complex.

The authors compared genes inside Salmonella pathogenicity islands across serovars. Some of these genes have evolved at different rates in different lineages. That divergence offers insight into how host specificity arises, linking the pace of gene change to which animals each strain can sicken. Host range is set by genes, and genes change at their own pace.
plos-pone-0003929:
An Li Wang, André Mouraux, Meng Liang, and co-authors studied a brain wave that grows when inputs come fast in 2008. The N1 wave is part of the brain's electric response to sound. Oddly, it grows when sounds repeat within 400 milliseconds. Most brain responses shrink with such rapid repeats instead.

Their PLOS ONE article asked whether that growth is a sound-only quirk. They tested whether other senses show the same effect. The boost turned out to be a general feature across sensory systems. The finding changes what researchers think the N1 wave is measuring.
plos-pone-0004029:
Neri Mercatelli, Valeria Coppola, Desirée Bonci, and co-authors blocked two small RNAs in prostate tumors in 2008. MiR-221 and miR-222 are small RNA regulators found at high levels in tumors. Their rise was reported in several human cancer types. One target they suppress is p27, a brake on the cell cycle.

Their PLOS ONE article reports blocking both RNAs impaired tumor growth in mice. The tumors were prostate carcinoma grafts grown in animals. Releasing the p27 brake likely explains part of the effect. The work supports microRNA blockers as a cancer drug idea. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004129:
Huan Zhang and Senjie Lin published this molecular biology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dinoflagellates are single-celled plankton, and they process their messenger RNA in an unusual way called trans-splicing. A short leader sequence, just 22 building blocks long, is cut from a small RNA and pasted onto the front of other RNA messages.

That leader had seemed to be missing in some dinoflagellates, which raised doubts about how universal the process is. Zhang and Lin report retrieving the missing spliced leader. Their finding supports the idea that this odd RNA step is a shared feature of the group. It also gives researchers a marker for finding genes in these organisms.
plos-pone-0004229:
Xiangqin Cui and Ann Loraine published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Affymetrix three-prime expression arrays carry thousands of redundant probe sets, groups of probes that question different regions of the same gene. Standard analysis methods rarely consider this redundancy, which can distort conclusions about a gene's overall activity.

The authors analyse how consistent these redundant probe sets are with each other. They also apply the results to detecting differential mRNA processing, where one gene yields differently cut messages. Their work helps analysts use the built-in repetition of these arrays instead of being misled by it.
plos-pone-0004329:
Yana Ilin and Gal Richter-Levin published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mood disorders affect millions of people each year. Large population studies link childhood trauma with higher rates of mood and anxiety disorders in adulthood. In rats, stress during juvenility, at 27 to 29 days of age, leaves lasting marks on learning and behaviour.

The team asked whether an enriched setting, a stimulating living space, can overcome those deficits. They report that enriched experience overcomes both the learning deficits and the depressive-like behaviour induced by juvenile stress. Good surroundings, in this model, can undo early damage.
plos-pone-0004429:
Tetrahymena thermophila is a single-celled creature long used as a model in biology. Wei Miao, Jie Xiong, Josephine Bowen, and co-authors charted its genes across its whole life cycle in PLOS ONE in 2009. It was the first ciliated protozoan to have its genome sequenced. That opened the door to reading gene activity across the full genome at once.

The team built a gene chip carrying the creature's predicted genes. With it, they tracked which genes switch on and off as the cell grows, starves, and mates. The resulting atlas gives other researchers a baseline for how this model organism runs its life. It also helps scientists who use Tetrahymena to ask basic questions about cells.
plos-pone-0004529:
Turning down a gene switch called ETS restores blood-vessel progenitor cells that diabetes depletes, report Florian Seeger, Linping Chen, and Ioakim Spyridopoulos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Transplants of vasculogenic progenitor cells, which help build new vessels, improve blood flow after tissue is starved of blood. But people with type 2 diabetes have fewer of these cells, and theirs work poorly.

Earlier work showed that blocking a stress enzyme, p38 kinase, could prevent some of the damage. This study goes upstream to ETS, a transcription factor family. Downregulating it rescued the progenitor cells that diabetes had reduced, as the title reports. Restoring a patient's own repair cells is an attractive path for treating diabetic damage to heart and limbs.
plos-pone-0004629:
Distant anchor points on DNA touch each other to keep a set of blood genes switched on, show Li Wang, Li-Jun Di, Xiang Lv, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genes are the human beta-globin cluster, which makes the protein chains of hemoglobin. Matrix attachment regions, or MARs, are DNA stretches that anchor chromatin to a nuclear scaffold and help organize genes.

Several MAR elements sit in the beta-globin cluster, but how they regulate the genes was unclear. The team shows associations between MARs contribute to looping events that keep the locus transcriptionally active. DNA looping brings far-apart switches next to the genes they control. Understanding that architecture helps explain blood disorders where globin genes are wrongly silenced.
plos-pone-0004729:
Kimberly Aldinger and colleagues mapped gene variation in outbred lab mice used across biomedicine, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Outbred mice are bred to stay varied, much like human groups. Yet little was known about how much variation they hold, so they were seldom used for gene studies.

The team focused on CD-1 mice, a common stock drawn from a very small founder group. They measured variation and subgroup structure in that stock. Knowing the true structure tells researchers when these mice suit gene hunts. It also warns where hidden subgroups could skew results. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004829:
Giovanna Franciosa and colleagues presented evidence that plasmid borne botulinum neurotoxin type B genes are widespread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plasmids encoding certain subtypes of botulinum neurotoxin type B were recently detected in some Clostridium botulinum strains. The objective was to investigate frequency of plasmid carriage of the toxin gene among serotype B strains from diverse sources and geographic origins tested.

Widespread plasmid carriage changes risk assessment for botulism. Mobile toxin genes can move between strains. Surveillance should track plasmids, not just species. Food safety and biodefense both benefit. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004929:
What sets the shape of a food web? The question is how living mass spreads among plants, herbivores and predators. Just Cebrian and colleagues took up that debate in PLOS ONE in 2009. They argued that producer quality is a controlling factor. Producer quality means the nutritional value of the plants at the base.

When plant food is poor in nutrients, each higher level supports less animal life. The authors link producer quality to key ecosystem values. These include stored carbon, nutrient cycling, and harvestable or rare species. The claim reframes food-web shape as a question of food quality. Predator numbers alone do not decide it.
plos-pone-0005029:
Turning genes on requires a giant helper called Mediator. It bridges activator proteins and the cell's copying machine, RNA polymerase II. Where Mediator binds in living yeast was controversial. Xiaochun Fan and Kevin Struhl mapped it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied yeast under optimal growth conditions.

Mediator is recruited to enhancer regions by activators. The map shows its real binding pattern in vivo. The pattern settles where Mediator sits when genes fire. Controversy had clouded a basic question of gene control. The answer grounds models of transcription in fact. It also guides work in more complex cells, where Mediator matters for development and disease.
plos-pone-0005129:
Some mice are bred to be anxious. Others are bred to be calm. Mirjam Bunck and colleagues searched their brains for the difference. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They compared high-anxiety and low-anxiety mouse lines. A weak version of the vasopressin gene stood out. Vasopressin is a brain chemical tied to social behavior.

The weak allele actually prevented anxiety-related behavior. Less vasopressin signaling meant calmer mice. That flips simple expectations about the gene. A hypomorphic allele reduces a protein's function partway. Here the partial reduction protects. The finding points to vasopressin as an anxiety lever. Drugs that tune it might calm human anxiety. The mouse lines give that idea a genetic foundation.
plos-pone-0005229:
A complex made from a milk protein, called HAMLET, can kill tumor cells while sparing healthy ones. Inside cells, the proteasome is the machine that chews up unwanted proteins. Gustafsson and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 how HAMLET changes that machine in tumor cells.

The study found changes in both the structure and the function of the proteasome after HAMLET treatment. Faulty protein clearance can itself push a cell toward death. Linking HAMLET to proteasome changes adds a new angle to how this unusual complex attacks tumors. That link also warns drug makers that a drug aimed at one part of the system may shift the rest in ways they must watch.
plos-pone-0005329:
Normal breast stem cells behave much like cancer stem cells, so studying the healthy ones informs cancer research. Human mammary stem and progenitor cells can be enriched by growing them in suspension. Dey and colleagues characterized those long-term cultures in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team described the cells' traits and functions after extended growth in the lab. A well-characterized culture system lets researchers test how normal breast stem cells divide and specialize. That baseline is what cancer stem cell claims must be compared against. Cells that keep their stem traits for months in a dish are a gift to labs, since each test can start from the same base stock and be checked side by side.
plos-pone-0005429:
Chun-Ting Zhang proposed a new way to score scientists in a 2009 PLOS ONE article. Many databases use the h-index, a single number based on how often a researcher's papers are cited. The number is simple and popular, but it ignores the extra citations earned by a person's most cited papers.

Zhang adds a partner number, the e-index, built from those extra citations. Used together, the two numbers give a fuller picture of a researcher's record. The proposal speaks to anyone who hires, funds, or judges scientists and wants a fairer way to compare their work.
plos-pone-0005529:
Einar Árnason, Ubaldo Benitez Hernandez, and Kristján Kristinsson warned of a cod fishery in trouble, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Cod choose habitats by type, and fishing hits some habitats harder than others. Heavy fishing in one habitat can act like a predator that favours certain gene forms there.

The authors found strong fishing-driven selection at one gene in a major cod stock. They argued that the trend points toward a near collapse of the fishery if it continues. Their warning links gene-level change to the fate of a whole industry.
plos-pone-0005629:
Hany Girgis, Alison Hottes, and Saeed Tavazoie mapped genes behind antibiotic sensitivity in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When bacteria meet an antibiotic, resistant strains quickly take over. The drug's chemistry and the cell's own networks both shape which mutations appear.

The team exposed a mutant library of bacteria to drugs and read which genes changed survival. The map shows the built-in weak points that decide a germ's starting sensitivity. Such maps can point to drug pairings that block escape routes to resistance. Maps of this sort also show which genes a germ can least afford to lose, a clue for new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0005729:
Scott Newman and co-authors tracked whooper swans across eastern Asia in 2009 and compared their routes with outbreaks of deadly bird flu. H5N1 flu kills wild birds and can threaten farms and people. Whether wild birds carry it long distances has been hotly debated.

The team used detailed movement data to line up swan travel with outbreak timing and place. Close matches would support a role for migrating swans; gaps would argue against it. Such checks help officials aim surveillance at the right birds and wetlands. They also keep blame for outbreaks grounded in evidence, not guesswork.
plos-pone-0005829:
Daniela Sarnataro and co-authors traced in 2009 how the normal prion protein enters cells. The prion protein, PrP, sits on cell surfaces; in prion diseases it converts to a rogue form that spreads. Entry into the cell seems required for that conversion.

Working in epithelial cells, the team found two routes cooperate: lipid rafts and clathrin-coated pits. Blocking either route changes how much protein gets inside. Knowing the entry path offers points to interrupt conversion early. The study adds cell-biology detail to a disease area often focused on the rogue protein alone.
plos-pone-0005929:
Baby birds beg for food with calls that vary from one moment to the next. Wan-chun Liu, Kazuhiro Wada and Fernando Nottebohm asked in 2009 whether that wobble means more than hunger. Their PLOS ONE paper treats varied begging calls as an early sign of vocal learning, the rare skill of copying sounds heard from others.

True imitation shows up late, so an early marker helps trace where the skill begins. If shaky begging calls come before learned song, then learning starts sooner than the first copied note. The work links a chick's first sounds to one of the rarest talents in birds and mammals, and it guides studies of how song develops.
plos-pone-0006029:
What kills most lung cancer patients is not the first tumor but its spread. Ulf Rapp, Christian Korn, Fatih Ceteci and colleagues named a driver of that spread in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies non-small-cell lung cancer, the most lethal human cancer thanks to its high rate of metastasis, and tests the Myc gene in a new animal model.

Myc acts as a metastasis gene for this cancer, the title reports. A gene that drives spread, separate from driving growth, is a distinct kind of target. The model also fills a long gap, since lung cancer's spread had lacked a good animal system in which to test ideas and drugs.
plos-pone-0006129:
The Wnt pathway is a master switch for growth, and cells keep several brakes on it. Lorna Kategaya, Binita Changkakoty, Travis Biechele and colleagues found a new brake in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper comes from a genome-wide RNAi screen in Drosophila cells carrying an active Wnt readout, hunting for parts that receive, pass on or end the Wnt signal.

The brake is a protein called Bili, which inhibits Wnt and beta-catenin signaling by regulating how Axin is recruited to LRP6, part of the signal's receiving complex. Each new brake on this pathway matters, since loose Wnt signaling drives common cancers. The screen also models how to hunt pathway parts at genome scale.
plos-pone-0006229:
A blood test for cancer would spare many patients invasive biopsies. Michael Lodes and colleagues tested tiny RNA molecules in blood serum as cancer signals, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These micro RNAs guide cell development, and their patterns differ between tissue types.

The team read the patterns with a chip carrying many small DNA probes. Cancer samples showed patterns the chip could detect and sort. Because each tissue leaves its own micro RNA fingerprint, blood may reveal where a cancer began. The study supports the wider push toward liquid biopsies for earlier, gentler diagnosis.
plos-pone-0006329:
Tuberculosis bacteria survive inside macrophages, the very cells meant to destroy them. Sarah Benson and Joel Ernst studied one evasion route in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The bacterium inhibits selected macrophage responses to interferon-gamma, a key activating signal, through a sensor called TLR2 and other routes.

TLR2-dependent inhibition works through distinct, gene-specific mechanisms, the authors show. Different defence genes are silenced in different ways, not by one blanket block. That precision helps explain the germ's staying power. It also gives researchers specific switches to target in new treatments.
plos-pone-0006429:
Tsuyoshi Tokusumi and colleagues used the fruit fly Drosophila to study blood cell formation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The fly is a strong model for the cell and gene sides of blood making. Healthy flies have two blood cell types, crystal cells and plasmatocytes. A third type, lamellocytes, appears when the fly faces certain threats.

The team characterized a gene switch, an enhancer, that helps turn on lamellocyte formation. The switch sits inside the misshapen gene. Mapping such switches shows how blood cell types are specified by genes. Fly work of this kind often points to shared rules in human blood development.
plos-pone-0006529:
Eric Campeau and co-authors built a versatile viral system for mammalian cells, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. The ability to express or deplete proteins in living cells is crucial for studying biological processes. Viral vectors are often useful to deliver DNA constructs to cells. The team aimed for one system that handles both adding and removing proteins.

A flexible system saves researchers from juggling incompatible tools. It also makes results across experiments easier to compare. Viral delivery reaches cell types that resist other methods. The paper is a practical resource for molecular biology labs.
plos-pone-0006629:
Margot Fournier and co-authors tested whether losing parkin changes a Parkinson's model in PLOS ONE in 2009. In synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, abnormal alpha-synuclein species accumulate. Parkin is a protein involved in clearing damaged proteins, and its loss causes some inherited Parkinson's. The team used a mouse model of synucleinopathy with parkin deficiency.

Their title reports parkin deficiency delays motor decline and disease manifestation in the model. That is the opposite of the expected harm. Surprising results like this force rethinking of how the two proteins interact. They caution against simple assumptions in combining genetic models.
plos-pone-0006729:
Fumiaki Imamura and Charles A. Greer studied how smell neurons grow their branches in PLOS ONE in 2009. The neurons are mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb. Their dendrites are shaped for efficient odor processing. A main dendrite reaches into a single glomerulus to receive input. Fine branching patterns determine how odors are sorted at this first relay.

The authors examined regulation of that branching by a receptor called TrkB. TrkB responds to growth signals that shape developing neurons. Changing TrkB activity changed how the dendrites branched. The work shows a molecular hand guiding smell circuit wiring. It helps explain how the nose's first map of odors is built.
plos-pone-0006829:
Ashesh Nandy searched for a pattern in the letter composition of conserved genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA sequences look like a formidably mixed string of four letters. Frequencies of those letters have been studied since Chargaff's rules. Conserved gene sequences are stretches kept similar by evolution. The author compared purine and pyrimidine counts within them.

Purines and pyrimidines are the two chemical families of DNA letters. An empirical relationship linked differences within each family. Such regularities can reveal constraints on sequence evolution. They also provide checks for sequence analysis methods. The finding adds to the statistical portrait of the genome's alphabet.
plos-pone-0006929:
Anna Bencsik, Sabine Debeer, Thierry Petit, and colleagues reported an animal disease case in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was feline spongiform encephalopathy, a prion disease of cats. The disease is considered related to bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle. Cases had appeared in domestic cats and captive wild cats, first in Britain, then elsewhere in Europe.

The case they describe involved a captive cheetah in France. Evidence pointed to possible transmission from mother to offspring. That route had not been clearly documented for this disease. The report matters for zoos and vets tracking prion diseases in rare captive animals.
plos-pone-0007029:
John Cho, Yun Kim, and Sherie Morrison screened for immune signal blockers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Host defense begins with complex signaling chains inside cells. Adaptors, kinases, and transcription factors pass the alarm along step by step. The chain ends in proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor, which rally the wider immune response.

The team used a new RNA interference screening method. They searched for what blocks cytokine output that depends on the adaptor MyD88. Found inhibitors are candidate starting points for anti-inflammatory drugs. They also map which links in the defense chain are truly required for the alarm to sound.
plos-pone-0007129:
Yanina Balabanova, Francis Drobniewski, Vladyslav Nikolayevskyy, and others tested fast TB diagnosis in Russia in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their region, Samara, had high rates of drug-proof TB. They paired liquid culture with gene-based tests for fast results. The aim was proof strong enough to shift world health policy on TB testing.

They weighed how well the paired system worked and what it cost. Speed counts, since drug-proof TB spreads while slow tests crawl. Their paired approach found drug resistance far sooner. Proof on both cost and results is what health leaders need before they change the rules for all clinics.
plos-pone-0007229:
Andrew D. Schweitzer, Robertha C. Howell, Zewei Jiang, and colleagues designed melanin materials as radiation shields in 2009. Melanin is a widespread natural pigment. Microorganisms rich in melanin can survive high doses of ionizing radiation, though the physics behind that protection was unknown.

The authors rationally designed new melanins and tested their physical and chemical properties. They evaluate the materials as nature-inspired radioprotectors. Such materials could one day shield people or equipment from radiation. Their study also probes how melanin interacts with ionizing radiation at a basic physical level. Their materials start from that familiar natural pigment.
plos-pone-0007329:
Abdoulaye Sene, Ramin Tadayoni, Thomas Pannicke, and colleagues studied a retinal protein involved in water balance in 2009. Müller cells are the principal glia of the retina.
