Changes in these cells are an early hallmark of most retinal diseases and help drive further progression of damage and vision loss.

Disturbed retinal homeostasis follows those Müller cell changes. The authors examine a protein called Dp71 in this context. They report functional implications for osmoregulation and vascular permeability in the retina. Their work links a structural protein to fluid control, a key issue in retinal swelling.
plos-pone-0007429:
Gabriel Martins and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the early embryo divides its body into segments. These segments, called somites, are temporary blocks that later give rise to vertebrae and muscles. In chick embryos a new pair forms about every ninety minutes. The team watched the process unfold in three dimensions.

They found that cells do not simply settle where they start. Instead, cells rearrange themselves in dynamic patterns as each segment takes shape. A mesh of the protein fibronectin surrounds them and guides the reshaping. The cells shift from a loose mass into an ordered epithelial block along that scaffold. The work shows segmentation as active choreography, not passive settling.
plos-pone-0007529:
Rekha Pattanayek and colleagues published a structural study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on KaiC, the clock protein of a cyanobacterium. The bacterium's daily clock can be rebuilt in a test tube from three proteins: KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC. KaiC tags and untags itself in a daily cycle, using three built-in enzyme activities. The team examined mutant versions of KaiC to learn how the machine works.

The structures revealed a new phosphorylation site, at position T426, where tags attach. They also clarified how the kinase, ATPase, and phosphatase activities fit together in one protein. Each activity plays a part in keeping the cycle's timing. Mutants that break one piece show what that piece contributes. The work refines the picture of the simplest known biological clock, atom by atom.
plos-pone-0007629:
Zhang Lei and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how tumors adapt when oxygen runs low. A master sensor called HIF-1 alpha drives the adaptation, switching on survival genes including VEGF, which grows new blood vessels. HIF-1 alpha was thought to be controlled mainly by a destruction pathway involving the pVHL protein. The discovery of microRNAs suggested another layer of control. The team tested one microRNA, miR-20b, in tumor cells.

MiR-20b regulates both HIF-1 alpha and VEGF. By tuning the sensor and its signal together, the small RNA adjusts how cancer cells weather oxygen shifts. That makes it a dial on the tumor's hypoxia response. Dialing it could, in principle, make tumors less able to survive their own growth. The finding adds microRNA control to a classic cancer pathway. It also gives drug hunters a new point of entry.
plos-pone-0007729:
Klaus Stark and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests whether gene variants that raise uric acid also raise disease risk. High uric acid can cause gout, a painful joint disease. It has also been suspected as a risk factor for coronary artery disease.

A large study of more than twenty-eight thousand people had found nine DNA sites tied to uric acid levels. This team checked whether those variants predict illness. They contributed to gout risk, as expected. They did not raise the risk of coronary artery disease, which argues uric acid itself may not cause heart disease.
plos-pone-0007829:
Guisheng Song and Li Wang published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the gene layout of two small RNAs, miR-433 and miR-127. MicroRNAs play essential roles in many cell processes. Yet little was known about how microRNA genes are structured and switched on.

The pair sits together in a gene cluster found across mammals. Using bioinformatics and lab tests, the authors mapped the cluster. They found a conserved structure and shared expression control. Conserved control hints the two RNAs work as a team. The work gives microRNA research a firmer map of its own genes.
plos-pone-0007929:
Emmanuel Mas and colleagues tested the role of a key immune signal in fatty liver disease, writing in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal is IL-6, a small protein that drives inflammation. Their mice were fed a diet that brings on steatohepatitis, a harsh form of fatty liver harm.

Mice bred to lack IL-6 fared better than normal mice on the same diet. Their livers showed less damage, which points to IL-6 as part of the problem rather than a bystander. The result names a target worth testing for a common liver illness that still has few good drug options.
plos-pone-0008029:
Anna Fabrega and colleagues built a drug-proof Salmonella strain and watched what it lost, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Salmonella causes gut illness worldwide, and strains that shrug off the fluoroquinolone drug family are a growing worry. Their mutant resisted those drugs at a very high level.

The resistant germs had dialed down their invasion genes for gut tissue, and they invaded poorly. Drug proofing came at a cost in attack strength. Such costs are common, and they matter: a strain that dodges drugs yet sickens less fiercely changes how doctors should weigh the threat.
plos-pone-0008129:
Kenneth Witwer and colleagues tracked how a monkey virus and the brain's defenses keep a long truce in PLOS ONE in 2009. SIV, the monkey kin of HIV, enters the brain early in infection. Yet brain illness usually comes late, which means something holds the virus down for years.

Brain readings showed virus growth and immune response rising and falling in step, a coordinated balance. As long as the response keeps pace, the brain stays sound. The study names what the balance rests on, and thus what its collapse, and late brain disease, may rest on too.
plos-pone-0008229:
Sergio Ruiz, Eugenio Santos, and Xosé R. Bustelo used knockout mice in a PLOS ONE study from 2009 on cancer genes. Vav1 and Rasgrf2 both help switch on Ras family proteins. They play roles in the development and action of T-lymphocytes. Mice lacking one or both genes had mostly been studied while young. The team followed older animals instead.

Mice missing both genes developed lymphomas and metastasis in a synergistic pattern. The combined loss did more than either loss alone. That reveals how two signaling faults can cooperate in cancer. The work may inform how lymphomas arise and spread.
plos-pone-0008329:
Yuanquan Song and colleagues studied a metabolic disorder in zebrafish and humans in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, or MADD, is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Mutations in the ETF or ETFDH genes cause it, also called glutaric aciduria type II. Patients face a broad spectrum of severe neurological and metabolic problems. The mechanisms behind those defects were the focus.

By studying zebrafish alongside human data, the team probed how the fault harms nerves and metabolism. Animal models reveal steps that patient studies cannot. Understanding the mechanism may guide future treatments.
plos-pone-0008429:
Bjorn Enzi and co-authors wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They ask if the sense of self is just a sense of reward. In daily life, people link sights and thoughts to themselves. That link gives a sense that things belong to them. Past work had tied that link to reward in the brain.

The authors scan the brain as people judge what feels close to self and what feels good. They look for brain areas that serve both tasks and areas that serve just one. They also link the results to traits of character. The work helps split self from reward, two ideas that are often mixed.
plos-pone-0008529:
Liguo Wang and co-authors present a statistical method for RNA sequencing in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. RNA-seq deeply sequences the transcriptome, all RNA messages in a cell. It offers an unprecedented chance to study alternative splicing. In splicing, exons are joined in different combinations to vary a message. Reads that span exon junctions reveal those combinations. Past studies counted junction reads in simple ways.

Their method models junction read counts with proper statistics. That improves detection of true alternative splicing events. It reduces false calls from uneven sequencing depth. The tool helps researchers read splicing patterns from RNA-seq data with more confidence.
plos-pone-0008629:
Cristina Olivieri and co-authors study errors in ancient DNA in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject is the Iceman, the ancient mummy found in the Alps. DNA degradation is a main issue in genetic analysis of archaeological specimens. A particular post-mortem modification causes nucleotide misincorporation, or miscoding lesions. Those lesions make sequencing read the wrong base at damaged sites. The team characterize misincorporation patterns in the Iceman's mitochondrial DNA.

Their patterns show where damage mimics true genetic variants. Knowing the pattern helps separate real mutations from decay artifacts. That distinction is vital for reconstructing ancient genomes accurately. The Iceman data become a benchmark for ancient DNA methods.
plos-pone-0008729:
Tomoki Yoshikawa, Terence Hill, Naoko Yoshikawa, and colleagues followed the first immune moves against the SARS virus. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung lining cells meet the virus before any other defense. Those bronchial cells can host viral growth. They can also release alarm chemicals that call in help. How that alarm unfolds over time was the question.

Infected human bronchial cells were sampled across the hours after infection. The team tracked which alarm signals rose and when. A timed map shows the lung's own early defense in action. Such maps help judge drugs that aim to calm harmful lung inflammation.
plos-pone-0008829:
Paul Denton, John Krisko, Daniel Powell, and colleagues showed HIV drugs given early can block infection in special mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The strategy is called pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. It aims to protect people at high risk before contact with the virus. Humanized BLT mice carry human immune cells, making them infectable. Both rectal and intravenous routes were tested.

Drugs given before exposure prevented HIV-1 transmission by both routes. Untreated mice became infected under the same challenges. A mouse proof strengthens the case for prevention trials in people. High-risk groups could gain a drug shield.
plos-pone-0008929:
Ricardo Gehrau and co-authors studied two opposing proteins in breast tumors for PLOS ONE in 2010. One, called KLF6, normally helps keep cell growth in check. The other, ERBB2, pushes cells to grow and is found at high levels in some breast cancers. The team focused on ductal carcinoma, the most common form of the disease.

They checked where KLF6 sits inside tumor cells, since it can only do its job in the nucleus. Tumors with lots of nuclear KLF6 also tended to carry high levels of ERBB2. That pairing was unexpected for a growth brake and a growth driver. It hints that KLF6 may behave differently once a tumor turns aggressive.
plos-pone-0009029:
Antonio Romito and co-authors showed a stress-sensing enzyme is needed to build heart cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, Sik1, belongs to a family that senses energy and salt stress. In mouse embryos, Sik1 marks the cell layer that will form the heart muscle. The team removed it from mouse embryonic stem cells.

Without Sik1, the stem cells largely failed to become beating heart cells. The failure traced to low levels of p57, a protein that brakes the cell cycle. Heart building apparently needs that brake applied at the right moment. The finding links energy sensing to the earliest steps of heart development.
plos-pone-0009129:
Desiree Tillo and co-authors overturned a rule of thumb about where gene switches sit, in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA wraps around protein spools called nucleosomes to form chromatin. In yeast, promoters and factor binding sites stay mostly spool-free and open. That openness was widely assumed to be the general pattern in eukaryotes.

Human regulatory DNA told a very different story, however. Promoters, enhancers, and binding sites carried high nucleosome occupancy instead. The crowding is encoded in the DNA sequence itself, the team showed. Human gene control apparently works with covered switches, quite unlike yeast.
plos-pone-0009229:
Ling Xue and colleagues published this immune cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines FoxM1, a protein that acts as a master switch for the cell cycle. In lab cell lines, losing FoxM1 delays division and scrambles chromosome counts. Inside the body, FoxM1 shows up mostly in cells that are actively growing.

The team tested where FoxM1 matters in T cells, the immune system's targeted fighters. They found it is a master regulator for mature T cells in mice. Surprisingly, it is not needed the same way in double positive thymocytes, an earlier stage of T cell development. The split shows that even master switches have stage-specific jobs.
plos-pone-0009329:
Jeffrey Martz and William Parker published this geology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It revisits the rock layers of Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona. The layers belong to the Sonsela Member of the Chinle Formation, laid down in the Upper Triassic. Recent work had proposed a three-part model for these rocks, based on unusual matches between sandstone beds.

The authors present a revised reading of that layered sequence. Getting the order right matters because animal fossils change within these very layers. A vertebrate faunal transition is recorded there, and its meaning depends on the rock framework. Their revision resets the stage for reading that ancient change.
plos-pone-0009429:
Wenming Qin and colleagues reported work in PLOS ONE in 2010 on tiny bits of RNA in cancer cells. These bits, called microRNAs, can lower the output of a gene after its message has been made. One such bit is miR-24. The group studied how miR-24 acts on a gene named FAF1, which helps cells die when they should.

Most microRNAs bind the tail end of a gene message. Qin's team found that miR-24 binds the middle, coding part of the FAF1 message instead. That binding cuts down FAF1 and changes cell death in cancer cells. The result widens the known ways that small RNAs can control genes.
plos-pone-0009529:
Luis Segu and co-authors tested memory in special mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with Alzheimer's disease have fewer serotonin 4 receptors in the brain. What that loss does to learning was not known. The team used mice born without those receptors. They set the mice a spatial memory task, the Morris water maze, which asks them to find a hidden platform.

Mice lacking the receptor kept their long term memory in the task. A second system, based on muscarinic receptors, had stepped up its activity. That backup kept memory working despite the missing part. The study shows the brain holds spare wiring for memory, a hopeful point for dementia research.
plos-pone-0009629:
Jianming Tang and co-authors tracked how immune genes relate to HIV levels over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. In untreated infection, the amount of virus in the blood settles at a level that predicts how fast disease advances. Genes called HLA, which present virus pieces to immune cells, help set that level. The team studied people from early infection into the chronic phase.

Links between HLA types and viral load changed as infection went on. Relationships seen early did not all hold later. That evolving pattern warns against judging a gene's effect at one time point only. It also deepens our picture of how the immune system and virus adjust to each other.
plos-pone-0009729:
Some bacteria can eat pollutants that poison soil and water. Athanasios Lykidis and colleagues read the full genome of one such microbe, Cupriavidus necator strain JMP134. The sequence appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The genome is multipartite, split across several separate DNA pieces.

A complete genome map shows every gene the microbe carries. Versatile degraders like this one can break down many kinds of waste chemicals. Knowing its full gene set helps scientists understand how it manages that range. The map also aids efforts to use the germ against toxic waste.
plos-pone-0009829:
Newspaper health stories shape what readers believe about medicine. Luca Iaboli and colleagues spent a week examining health science reporting in Italian print media. Their review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. They judged how deep and how accurate the coverage ran.

Light reporting can skip risks, uncertainty, and the limits of a study. The team cataloged what a week of print coverage got right and wrong. Findings like these show editors where health pages fall short. Better reporting helps readers make sounder health choices. One week gave the team a snapshot of everyday practice.
plos-pone-0009929:
A few extra building blocks at one end of a protein can change whether it clumps. Marc Erhardt and colleagues showed that effect in a potential yeast prion protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The protein is Mca1, a candidate prion in yeast. Prions are proteins that fold wrongly and seed clumping in others. Aggregation means proteins sticking together in clumps. Extra N-terminal residues, added at the protein's front end, had a profound effect on aggregation. Small changes at the edge thus decide whether the protein stays soluble.
plos-pone-0010029:
The authors were Sverker Lundin, Henrik Stranneheim, Erik Pettersson, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper tackled a bottleneck in DNA sequencing. Modern machines read DNA very fast. Preparing samples for them stayed slow, hands-on work that could hold up a whole project.

The team sped up sample preparation by running many preparations in parallel. More samples could then move through the same step at once, raising throughput. Faster preparation means sequencing projects, from gene surveys to medical tests, can finish sooner at lower cost. The paper reports the setup in practical, step-by-step detail.
plos-pone-0010129:
The authors were Yuan-Ping Pang, Jon Davis, Shaohua Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study searched for drugs against botulinum toxin. Serotype A of that toxin causes botulism, a life-threatening paralysis. A deliberate release could harm large unprotected groups, and post-exposure care was limited to support and symptoms.

The team identified small molecules that gave mice significant protection against the toxin. A drug that works after exposure would fill a clear gap in preparedness. The findings offer starting points for further testing, not a ready human treatment. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010229:
Barbara Ballentine and Russell Greenberg compared two swamp sparrow subspecies in 2010. The two forms look different, though their neutral DNA shows little divergence. Strong selection on key traits can drive such visible divergence while gene flow continues. Relying on neutral DNA alone would miss these distinct populations in conservation surveys of wild birds.

In a common garden experiment, both forms were raised under the same conditions. Differences that persisted there point to genetic control of the divergence. Their PLOS ONE study shows form can be inherited even when marker DNA looks much the same.
plos-pone-0010329:
Lan Wang, Mark Clark, David Crossman and others analyzed drusen, small deposits tied to aging eyes, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Drusen build up under the retina and mark age-related macular disease, a leading cause of vision loss in older people. The team wanted a full account of what these deposits contain. They measured the shares of fats and proteins in real samples.

Samples came from drusen capped with the pigment cell layer behind the retina. The authors compared them with that same cell layer taken from healthy parts of the eye. Fats and proteins both proved plentiful in the deposits. Knowing the recipe of drusen helps explain how they form. It may also point to steps that could be slowed or stopped.
plos-pone-0010429:
Eric Lind and John Parker tested whether invading plants are better armed with chemicals than natives, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A leading idea says invaders succeed because their chemistry is new to local enemies. Native insects and fungi have no defenses against unknown poisons. Despite the idea's fame, direct experimental tests were lacking. The team compared chemical defenses of invasive and native plants head-to-head.

Experiments, not just surveys, can say whether invaders truly invest more in defense. If they do not, other explanations for invasion take priority. Plant invasions reshape whole food webs for decades. Knowing the real mechanism helps managers predict which newcomers will explode. This study puts a popular theory to a fair test.
plos-pone-0010529:
Gavin Collett and co-workers showed that lowering a scaffolding protein makes placenta-type cells fuse more in PLOS ONE in 2010. During pregnancy, placental cells fuse into a shared layer that faces the mother's blood. That fusion is essential for a healthy pregnancy. Its failure is linked to pre-eclampsia and poor fetal growth. The team studied a human cell line that models this fusion, called BeWo.

Reducing caveolin-1, a protein that shapes cell surface pockets, increased fusion. A brake on fusion, once lifted, lets the process run faster. Knowing the brakes and accelerators of placental fusion could explain pregnancy complications. It may also suggest ways to support failing placentas. The study adds one clear control to a vital process.
plos-pone-0010629:
Lucia Zacchi and colleagues cut the supply of a DNA-packaging protein in a yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The yeast, Candida albicans, causes infections in people with weak immunity. Its DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the amount of each histone must stay balanced.

Lowering histone H4 slowed growth and changed cell shape. The cells also handled their chromosomes less reliably. In Candida, chromosome mistakes are tied to drug resistance, so packaging balance matters beyond basic growth. The study shows how tightly this pathogen's survival depends on exact protein amounts.
plos-pone-0010729:
Qing Cai and Marc Brysbaert built a Chinese word frequency list from film subtitles, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Word frequency shapes almost every language experiment, from reading speed to memory. Chinese researchers had few good frequency sources, and the existing ones rested on limited text.

Subtitles capture speech as people actually use it, including daily words that books miss. The team counted words and single characters across a large subtitle collection. The counts predicted experiment results better than older lists. SUBTLEX-CH quickly became a standard tool for Chinese language science, much as subtitle lists had for English and other languages.
plos-pone-0010829:
Douglas Cork, Steven Lembark, Sodsai Tovanabutra and co-authors described a computing method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their tool uses the W-curve, a way of drawing DNA sequences as shapes, to compare whole virus genomes. They applied it to HIV-1, the virus that causes AIDS, whose genome is notoriously hard to line up with standard methods.

Gaps and heavy mutation, especially in the envelope gene, slow ordinary string-based alignment of HIV-1. The W-curve approach compares sequences in a single pass, without recursion, so it runs fast and handles many samples at once. Cork and colleagues were tuning the method for the quirks of HIV-1 genomes. A quicker way to track how the virus changes could support both diagnosis work and vaccine design.
plos-pone-0010929:
Radu Minea, Corey Helchowski, Samuel Zidovetzki and co-authors published this cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Disintegrins, proteins from snake venom, can block integrins, the anchors cells use to grip tissue and blood vessels, and they have slowed tumors in animals. Making them in the lab is notoriously hard because their many internal bonds must pair exactly right.

The team engineered a chimera called vicrostatin and produced it reliably at scale inside modified bacteria. The molecule grabs three integrin types at once, hitting both tumor cells and the endothelial cells that build new blood vessels. Through a recreated tissue barrier it sharply reduced cell movement, and it also showed vessel-starving and cell-death effects. Minea and colleagues turn a finicky venom protein into a manufacturable drug candidate.
plos-pone-0011029:
Samantha McNulty, Jeremy Foster, Makedonka Mitreva and co-authors published this parasite genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wolbachia bacteria live inside most filarial worms, the parasites behind elephantiasis and river blindness, and the worms depend on them to develop and survive. A few worm species are naturally Wolbachia-free, and the authors wondered whether they were always so.

Sequencing surveys of two unrelated Wolbachia-free species found dozens to over a hundred stretches of Wolbachia-like DNA embedded in the worm genomes, and many of those sequences were actively being read. McNulty and colleagues read this as fossil evidence of ancient infections whose genes jumped into the worm's own chromosomes. The discovery complicates using Wolbachia as a drug target, and shows symbiont DNA can linger as a permanent inheritance.
plos-pone-0011129:
Beckers and Gahr recorded songbird brains in PLOS ONE in 2010. Songbirds talk with calls that often repeat the same sounds. The authors asked how hearing centers in the bird brain handle sounds that recur within a short time.

Brain responses showed a tuned handling of repeated versus new sounds. That tuning helps a bird pick out fresh calls in a stream of familiar ones. The work adds to hearing science in a model animal whose vocal learning is well studied. It also hints at general rules the brain uses to flag change and ignore routine noise.
plos-pone-0011229:
Mensch, Carreira, Lavagnino and colleagues compared mountain fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flies living at different heights grow up at different speeds, since cold slows development. The team tested candidate timing genes for effects that appear only at certain life stages along that height gradient.

Stage specific effects showed that timing genes do not act evenly across a fly's life. A gene may speed one stage and leave another untouched. That nuance helps explain how populations adapt development to altitude. It also refines the study of how evolution tunes life history in changing climates.
plos-pone-0011329:
Paul Haggarty and colleagues asked in 2010 whether genes that tag DNA help explain why people differ in thinking ability. They focused on four genes that add chemical marks to DNA, a process linked to how genes are switched on or off. Such marks had been tied to syndromes with severe mental impairment, but their role in normal variation was unclear.

The group measured common variants in the four genes and compared them with scores of general intelligence. By testing healthy people rather than patients, the study asks whether the same tagging system also shapes ordinary differences in ability. The results give behavioral genetics a careful check on a tempting idea, and they show how hard it is to pin a complex trait on a few gene variants.
plos-pone-0011429:
Lars Bochmann and co-authors hunted in 2010 for new marker genes that identify the heart's outer layer. The epicardium, a thin skin over the heart, holds cells that help build and repair heart tissue, yet researchers lacked reliable tags to find those cells among many others. The team read the full set of active genes in mouse epicardial cells.

Comparing that profile with other tissues revealed new markers that single these cells out with confidence. Fresh tags let researchers isolate living epicardial cells and follow what they do after a heart injury. That ability is a basic need for regenerative research, since a repair cell cannot be studied or guided until it can be found. The paper supplies the field with handles it had been missing.
plos-pone-0011529:
Amelia Guadalupe-Grau and co-authors tested in 2010 whether stutter-like repeats in a hormone gene track with bone strength in young men. The androgen receptor, which senses male hormones, contains two repeat stretches whose length varies between people and tunes how strongly the receptor answers. Since male hormones help build bone, the team asked whether repeat length predicts bone mass.

Measuring bone mass in young men alongside their receptor repeats lets the study catch the skeleton near its peak, before age and illness muddy the picture. Any link found there points to a lifelong, built-in influence on fracture risk. The question matters because peak bone mass is the savings account a man draws on for the rest of his life. Genetic contributors to that peak are worth knowing while building is still possible.
plos-pone-0011629:
Sarah Straud and co-authors asked why some cancer cells die easily under a certain drug class, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drugs block V-ATPases, pumps that keep the inside of cells at the right acidity. Many tumour cell lines are far more sensitive to these blockers than normal cells, for reasons that were unknown.

Using gene activity data across cell lines, the team traced the difference to iron. Blocking iron uptake proved responsible for the uneven sensitivity. The link turns a drug puzzle into a question of cell metabolism, and it hints that iron handling could predict which tumours these drugs might help.
plos-pone-0011729:
Hanna Irie and co-authors studied how tumour cells survive without anchorage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Normal cells die when detached from their surroundings, but tumour cells that can survive floating free are thought to seed spread to new sites. Proteins required for that trick are attractive drug targets.

The team showed a protein called PTK6 regulates survival of detached cells when the growth factor IGF-1 signals. Removing that support undermines the free-floating state. Exposing this lifeline gives researchers a specific dependency of drifting tumour cells that treatment might sever.
plos-pone-0011829:
Natalia Cheshenko and co-authors studied how herpes simplex virus seizes the cell's protein works, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stopping genital herpes is a top health goal across the world. A common human protein had been put forward as a door the virus uses to enter cells, and the team probed its role in infection.

They found the virus takes over subunit M of initiation factor 3, one gear of the protein-making works, to build its own proteins. Weakening that gear cut virus plaque growth sharply in their tests. The seized part marks a fresh target for blocking the virus.
plos-pone-0011929:
Salomon Kuizon and co-workers pinned down in 2010 two things an enzyme must have to do its job, an enzyme whose loss causes a fatal brain disease of childhood. The enzyme, known by the short name TPPI, breaks down proteins inside the cell's waste sacs. Children born without a working copy develop a cruel, steady loss of brain function in their first years.

From the enzyme's known shape, the team found a key building block, a tryptophan, and a need for calcium in both the enzyme's start-up and its cutting work. Knowing which parts it cannot do without sharpens the search for what goes wrong in sick children. It also sets the terms any stand-in enzyme would have to meet to work as a cure.
plos-pone-0012029:
Rohan Patil and co-workers argued in 2010 that the weakest forces in nature decide whether a drug can do its job. Two such forces hold a drug in the pocket of its target protein: hydrogen bonds, a mild pull between atoms, and the push of water-fearing parts to hide from water. How the mix of those forces sets grip strength was still not well mapped.

By studying many drug and target pairs, the team drew design rules from the way snug water-fearing contact and well-placed hydrogen bonds work as a team. In plain terms, bury the parts that fear water and place each bond with care. Rules of that sort help drug makers lift a weak lead to a strong one with less blind trial and error.
plos-pone-0012129:
Xiaoxia Peng, Shige Song, Sheena Sullivan, and co-authors tracked disability trends in China across nineteen years, in PLOS ONE in 2010. As populations age, disability rises, and rural areas usually carry more of it than cities. China changed faster than almost any country in that span, growing older and more urban at once, which makes its record a natural test of how those forces interact.

Using national data from the late nineteen eighties to the mid two thousands, they weighed ageing against the urban-rural gap. The trends show where disability grew fastest and for whom. Such evidence helps a vast country plan care, pensions, and services for the older and disabled people who need them most.
plos-pone-0012229:
Elena Braithwaite, Padmini Kedar, Deborah Stumpo, and co-authors compared two DNA repair enzymes in mouse cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Every day, small chemical dents appear in DNA bases, and a repair pathway called base excision repair fixes them. One polymerase enzyme does most of that pathway's rebuilding work, but evidence suggested a cousin enzyme can step in as backup.

Using embryonic mouse cells missing one or both enzymes, the team separated where their jobs overlap and where each works alone. Backup systems explain why losing one repair gene is often survivable. They also matter in cancer, where tumor cells lean on backups to resist DNA-damaging drugs.
plos-pone-0012329:
Xavier Durrmeyer, Shushanik Hovhannisyan, Yves Médard, and co-authors asked if gene variants explain ibuprofen failures in preterm babies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Very early babies often keep a fetal blood vessel open. That vessel should close soon after birth. Ibuprofen is the standard drug to close it. Yet it fails in up to four babies in ten. Two liver enzymes break the drug down. The genes for those enzymes vary between people.

Testing those variants in very preterm infants checks one clear idea. Slow or fast drug handling may decide whose vessel closes. If genes explain the failures, doctors could pick the dose by a quick test. They could also switch drugs at once instead of losing days. In care of newborns, days are not a small currency.
plos-pone-0012429:
Kathrin Wippel, Anke Wittek, Rainer Hedrich and colleagues compared sugar transporters in plants and fungi, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Plants move sucrose, their main transport sugar, through special carrier proteins. Fungi that infect plants run similar carriers to steal that sugar. Both respond to acidity around them, raising the question of who wins when conditions change.

The team found the plant and fungal carriers react to acidity in opposite ways. As one speeds up, the other slows, a tug of war at the host-pathogen border. That switch could be a target for crop protection: tilt the balance so the plant keeps its sugar and the invader starves.
plos-pone-0012529:
Chen Zhang, Antony Jackson, Zai-Rong Zhang and colleagues fed yeast prion clumps to vertebrate cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ure2 is a yeast protein that can fold into amyloid, the stacked clump form behind many human diseases. How such clumps get into cells and whether they harm foreign species were open questions with safety implications.

The clumps entered vertebrate cells through specific endocytotic routes and induced the cells to die by apoptosis. A yeast amyloid harming animal cells shows these clumps are broadly toxic, not species-bound curiosities. The uptake routes identified may be the same doors human amyloids use, suggesting shared points for blocking them.
plos-pone-0012629:
Dhodda, Godiska, VanWye and co-authors presented a cheaper way to copy DNA in the lab. The standard method, PCR, needs costly enzyme added to each reaction. Their 2010 paper describes cells, sold as ExCyto PCR cells, that carry the heat-proof enzyme gene inside their own chromosomes.

Bacteria holding the DNA of interest grow and make the enzyme themselves, giving strong, hot-start copying at lower cost. Cheaper copying helps small labs, schools and clinics that run many DNA tests. The method turns the host cell into both the storage and the factory.
plos-pone-0012729:
Shin, Martin, Kim and co-authors found a hunger hormone at work inside taste buds. Ghrelin is best known as a stomach signal that stirs appetite. Their 2010 study showed taste cells themselves make ghrelin, and that mice lacking its receptor respond less to salty and sour tastes.

Taste shapes what animals eat, so a hormone acting in the tongue ties hunger to flavour directly. The finding may help explain why appetite states change how food tastes. It also adds taste buds to the list of places metabolic hormones act.  Salt and sour responses were tested separately in the mice.
plos-pone-0012829:
Harscoet, Dubreucq, Palauqui and co-authors named a plant protein that controls how much ribosomal RNA a cell makes. Ribosomes build all proteins, so their output must match the cell's growth plans. Their 2010 study of arabidopsis describes NOF1, a protein based in the nucleolus where ribosomal RNA is produced.

Plants with altered NOF1 changed their ribosomal RNA expression, showing its control role. Getting this control wrong would throttle growth at the source. The finding adds a named part to a process every plant cell depends on.  The protein was tracked through the cell's nucleolus directly.
plos-pone-0329429:
Belay Berza Beyene and co-authors survey helpful soil fungi living on tree roots in two dry mountain forests in northwestern Ethiopia. These fungi trade soil nutrients and water to trees in exchange for sugars, and they can help trees survive stress. The team collected soil from around the roots of dominant tree species across both forests during the dry season and sieved out fungal spores.

Spore counts and variety differed by forest and by host tree, with one forest holding richer and denser communities. A single fungal genus appeared on nearly every host sampled. Certain trees, including a native acacia and a planted cypress, hosted the widest mix. Beyene and colleagues suggest those trees and their fungi could support efforts to restore damaged mountain forests.
plos-pone-0329529:
Océane Amichaud and colleagues tested whether cows recognize individual people, even across senses. Thirty-two cows watched pairs of silent videos, one of a familiar person and one of a stranger. In a second test the videos played with a voice that either matched or clashed with the face on screen.

Cows looked longer at the stranger's video, showing they could tell the faces apart visually. When voice and face were paired, they looked longer at the combination that matched, proof they hold a joined mental picture of a person, not just a face or a voice alone. Farm animals' ability to know their handlers matters for welfare, since familiar, predictable humans mean calmer animals.
plos-pone-0333729:
Sarvar, Coombe, and Birol presented a data tool for spotting errors in assembled genomes in a 2026 paper. Reading a genome from millions of short pieces can join pieces wrongly, and those mistakes corrupt later research. Their structure stores short DNA chunks in a compact hashed form built for huge data sets.

A filled structure can test whether two genome pieces truly belong near each other. Mismatches flag likely assembly errors for repair. The design aims to use far less memory than older stores while staying fast to query. Cleaner assemblies matter because gene hunts, disease studies, and breeding work all build on the assembled sequence.
plos-pone-0342629:
Alice Coffey, Robert Lillywhite, and Oyinlola Oyebode weighed the diets of thirty-nine British children aged two to twelve, omnivores, vegetarians, and vegans, on two scales at once: nutrition and climate cost. Three-day weighed food diaries fed nutrient software, and each ingredient carried its greenhouse gas price. Parents of plant-based children often face claims their choices starve growth, claims worth checking with real diaries.

No group hit every nutrient target. Omnivores overshot saturated fat and sugar and missed fiber, while plant-based children sat in the healthy range on those. Plant diets covered protein and B12 even without supplements, and vegans alone met iron targets from food. Vitamin D and zinc fell short widely. Emissions told a clean story: vegans lowest, at nearly half the omnivore footprint. Careful planning, not the label, made the difference.
plos-pone-0343029:
Hameed Ali and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One methods paper on control charts. These charts watch factory processes for early signs of trouble. Many safety-critical measures, like failure times and repair times, follow a skewed pattern. Standard charts handle such data poorly. The authors propose a chart that tracks both the mean level and the spread at the same time.

Their design adds safeguards so the chart still behaves when the assumed data pattern is wrong. It also copes when sensors add noise. The chart adjusts how often samples are taken, based on cost and delay. In computer tests it spotted real problems faster than standard charts. A chip factory case shows how the method could guide repairs in real plants.
plos-pone-0345429:
Stéphanie Mottier and seven colleagues question a basic assumption about a rare, aggressive cancer in dogs, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Histiocytic sarcoma spreads through the body, and doctors usually assume every tumour in one dog descends from a single original. The team compared driver mutations in tumour pairs taken from the belly and chest of thirty-eight dogs with the widespread form.

In several dogs the two sites carried different mutations in the same cancer gene — something spread from one source cannot explain. After correcting for what their test can miss, they estimate a large share of cases may begin as separate cancers. That changes how the disease should be treated and studied.
plos-pone-0346829:
Xiangui Bu and co-authors surveyed more than twelve hundred athletes to learn how a coach's style shapes sportsmanship. Coaches can lead democratically, sharing decisions, or in an authoritarian way that demands obedience. The 2026 questionnaire study measured both leadership styles alongside athletes' helpful and harmful behavior toward others, their goal focus, and their willingness to excuse bad conduct.

Democratic leadership went with more helpful behavior and less harmful behavior, while authoritarian leadership showed the reverse pattern. Both styles also worked indirectly: they shifted what athletes aimed for and how easily they excused misconduct, and those shifts in turn moved behavior. The authors advise coaches to share more decisions, steer athletes toward mastery goals, and challenge excuses for dirty play.
plos-pone-0347029:
Celmira Laza-Vásquez and colleagues interviewed twelve health professionals working on MyPeBS, a European trial of personalised breast screening, about a delicate proposal: women at low risk would be screened less often. Longer intervals free resources for higher-risk women, but professionals must judge whether patients will accept stepping back from a familiar routine.

The professionals expected relief at a low-risk label but uneven acceptance of fewer mammograms, shaped most by how faithfully a woman had attended screening before. They raised open questions about real benefit, fairness, and staffing costs. The authors recommend research with women themselves and careful communication before any program stretches intervals for low-risk groups.
plos-pone-0347129:
Maquet and colleagues compared how medical students and family doctors reason through sudden dizziness in a 2026 French study. Dizziness is common in front-line care, yet telling a harmless cause from a stroke risk is tricky. Both groups answered the same case-based tests, which score judgment on realistic patient stories.

Final-year students scored higher on the reasoning tests than working doctors did. Among doctors, higher scores went with seeing fewer patients each day, past extra training on dizziness, and stronger confidence in handling it. The gap suggests that skills taught in school fade without refreshers. Short update courses for busy doctors could help close that gap.
plos-pone-0347329:
Paula Tavrow and colleagues tested a low-cost way to draw rural Kenyan teenagers into sexual and reproductive health services. Young people often avoid clinics for fear of judgement, gossip, and being spotted by relatives. The After-Hours project kept thirteen government clinics open into the early evening and staffed them with newly trained young nurses, some of whom also taught classes in nearby schools.

After one year, youth visits at project clinics rose by eighty-seven percent, while comparison sites stayed flat. Clinics where nurses also taught in schools gained the most, attracting younger and more female clients. Nurses' attitudes toward young clients improved and stayed improved. The catch is ongoing salary costs, the authors note.
plos-pone-0347429:
Asma Alshanqiti and colleagues surveyed three hundred eighty-nine female secondary school students in Madinah, Saudi Arabia, about sexual and reproductive health knowledge. In conservative settings such knowledge is often uneven, and mothers and school type may shape what girls learn. The questionnaire covered menstruation, anatomy, contraception, relationships, and disease awareness, plus how much parents and daughters talk about these topics.

The weakest knowledge clustered in contraception and relationships, and some students wrongly believed casual contact spreads sexually transmitted diseases. Private school students scored higher than government school students, and a mother's education was clearly linked to her daughter's knowledge. The pattern shows where school health teaching and parent support could close the largest gaps.
plos-pone-0347929:
Manting Wang and colleagues reviewed the mathematical models built since 2023 to simulate highly pathogenic bird flu, the virus family behind devastating poultry outbreaks and occasional human infections. Searching the major databases, their 2026 scoping review kept thirty studies and sorted them by model type, hosts covered, and purpose.

Compartmental models, which shuffle populations between health states, dominated; only a handful used agent-based or network approaches that capture individual behaviour and farm-to-farm contacts. Livestock such as cattle, now known to catch the virus, were rarely modelled, and few studies wove in real outbreak data. The authors list these gaps as priorities before the next pandemic scare.
plos-pone-0348129:
Alireza Yousefi Kebriya and co-workers trace dust storms over Iran's Khuzestan province across five years, using satellite readings, ground monitors, and wind path modeling. Dust chokes air quality and harms lungs across the region. Their 2026 study links satellite haze measures with fine particle counts on the ground and follows air parcels backward to find where dust starts.

Satellite and ground readings agreed closely, confirming remote tracking works. The main dust highway crossed eastern Iraq, and most paths passed over Iraqi deserts. A great border wetland shrank dramatically over the period, and its size tracked dust levels strongly. Below a size threshold, dust worsened sharply. Restoring wetlands emerges as part of any serious dust defense.
plos-pone-0348529:
Carsten Neumann counts the white ray petals of common daisies across Brandenburg, Germany, in this 2026 study, testing a piece of botanical folklore. Textbooks often imply that flower structures follow the Fibonacci sequence neatly. Between April and May 2024 he sampled more than five hundred daisies from thirty-four populations and built statistical models of how petal counts are distributed.

Most flower heads carried between thirty-four and fifty-six rays, peaking in the low forties, and the counts followed a smooth probability distribution rather than a tidy sequence. Two precise exceptions stood out: counts of thirty-four and fifty-five, both Fibonacci numbers, occurred more often than the smooth model predicts. Neumann names this pattern improbable recurrency, deterministic fingerprints detectable only inside randomness, and argues it captures how order and chance jointly shape natural forms.
plos-pone-0348629:
Fereshteh Khaleghdadi and co-authors studied breeding timing in urial wild sheep across six protected areas of Iran in 2026. As the climate shifts, mating and birth must still land when food peaks, or lambs suffer.

Weather records near each site, plus height and location, were matched to observed mating and lambing dates. Timing differed clearly between regions, and heat and rain patterns helped explain the gaps. Sheep in some areas already breed off the old schedule. The results warn managers that protected herds may drift out of sync with spring growth, with costs for lamb survival and herd links.
plos-pone-0348729:
Sharon Akinyi Okoth, Festus M Njuguna, and colleagues examined blood cells from children in western Kenya to understand a long-noted link between malaria and Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt lymphoma is a fast-growing cancer of white blood cells and a leading cause of child cancer deaths in parts of Africa. Their 2026 study compared children exposed to malaria, children with the lymphoma, and adults with little malaria exposure.

Using a lab method that sorts cells by surface markers, the team found that malaria-exposed children carried more aged and immature neutrophils, a type of infection-fighting cell. Children with the lymphoma showed a similar rise in immature cells. The authors suggest that malaria may reshape these cells in ways that help the cancer take hold.
plos-pone-0349429:
Rokonuzzaman and co-authors surveyed more than one thousand folks in the drug trade in Dhaka, Bangladesh. The land sits between big drug-making zones, and the trade lives on past police work. Their 2026 study used face-to-face talks, with chain links to reach a hidden group, plus world data on trade webs.

Folk averaged in their late twenties, and most had primary school at best. The mix held a shock: women and kids aged fifteen and under formed a big share. Street life and sex work were both rife in the group. Rokonuzzaman and colleagues say policy must face a trade staffed in part by the poor and used, not just by crime chiefs.
plos-pone-0349829:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One editors have retracted the article this notice concerns, which had claimed links between going hungry and poor mental health for women in a developing country under COVID-19. After publication, critics raised doubts about how participants were sampled, whether the analysis was valid and reliable, whether the results could be reproduced, and whether the data supported the conclusions.

The journal's follow-up found that stress questionnaire items needing reverse scoring appear to have been coded incorrectly, making some high-stress answers read as low stress. The underlying coding files were unavailable, and figures, tables, and text disagreed with each other in several places. Readers should not rely on the original article's findings.
plos-pone-0350129:
Zhenmei Song and colleagues explored how low oxygen at high altitude harms gut lining cells through a fat driven form of cell death. A protein that coats fat droplets inside cells, switched on by low oxygen sensors, was the prime suspect. Human stomach and gut cells were grown under low oxygen, with the sensors and the suspect protein raised or lowered in turn.

Raising the sensors or the protein worsened cell death, while a death blocking drug reversed it. Lowering the protein cut fat damage and restored cell power units. Fat profiles showed the protein loads cell membranes with fragile fats via a partner enzyme. Blocking that chain may protect travellers and workers at altitude.
plos-pone-0350229:
Qi and colleagues tuned a soil treatment that flows like liquid then hardens in a 2026 study. The binder is a geopolymer made from slag and fly ash, mixed into wind-blown soil. Four ingredients were varied: binder share, water ratio, fiber, and alkali dose, with flow and strength measured after curing.

More binder cut flow sharply but more than doubled strength. More water raised flow greatly, while strength peaked at a middle water ratio. Microscope images helped explain the patterns. Such pourable soil suits filling and ground repair where packing is hard, while using industrial byproducts instead of cement cuts the footprint.
plos-pone-0350429:
Emad Hafaf and colleagues built a combined way to judge why shop shelves and warehouses run out of stock. Long waits for supplies are a prime suspect. Their data covered twenty thousand supply incidents. They paired methods that try to isolate cause with machine learning models that forecast trouble, plus simple time trend forecasts.

Matching like cases with like cases gave the most trusted estimate, and it showed a strong causal link from longer wait times to higher stockout risk. A different check using distance to suppliers as a lever gave a weaker, unclear result. Tree based learning models forecast best among the learning tools. Managers get a practical lesson here: cut waiting time first, and use forecasts to act before shelves empty.
plos-pone-0350629:
Shihao Zhang and co-authors watched grout spread through coarse soil material, a process that normally stays hidden underground. Grout is pumped into earth dams to seal and strengthen them, but lost fine particles can distort how it flows. Their 2026 lab study used transparent artificial soil and dyed resin so cameras could track the flow, with three mixes holding different amounts of fine particles.

Too many fines clogged the pores, forcing grout upward and leaving only patchy, blocky bonding. With no fines at all, grout sank fast under gravity and barely spread sideways. A middle amount gave the best result, an even ball of grout that glued large grains at contact points and filled small gaps. The findings help engineers tune dam repairs to the soil actually in place.
plos-pone-0350729:
Ordering spare parts for a brand-new product is guesswork, because no sales history exists yet. Sendhil Nathan B and co-authors built a forecasting method for exactly this cold start, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper using real industrial order data.

Their approach splits the problem in two: first, will any demand happen at all, and second, how large might it be. A coin-flip style model handles the first question and a skewed curve the second, then repeated random sampling builds a full range of possible demand. Tested so that every part was genuinely unseen, the method beat strong single-model rivals, giving stock planners a clearer view of risk.
plos-pone-0350829:
Wenhan Yang analysed breast cancer data from two large cohorts in 2026, asking whether low oxygen inside tumors predicts survival and tracks genetic damage. Oxygen shortage is known to make cancers nastier, but its signal may just reflect tumor subtype.

In one cohort, the survival link vanished once subtype and clinical factors were counted, except in one subtype where low oxygen meant better survival after adjustment. In the second cohort, high oxygen shortage still meant worse survival under a different model. Higher shortage also tracked heavier chromosome damage throughout. The mixed picture warns against using oxygen scores without subtype context.
plos-pone-0350929:
Idongesit Aniekan Ekpo and colleagues packed a common cancer drug into tiny balls made from chitosan, a material from natural sources. The drug, called 5-FU in short, harms healthy cells as well as cancer cells and can lose effect over time. Tiny carriers aim to bring more drug into cancer cells and less elsewhere. Lab checks used breast cancer cells grown in dishes.

Balls averaged a little over two hundred nanometres wide and held a modest share of drug, released slowly by diffusion. Checks confirmed the drug sat inside with a round shape. Killing of breast cancer cells grew stronger the longer cells were exposed, over three days. Dish results cannot prove patient benefit, but they support more work on the carrier.
plos-pone-0351029:
Shuo Yang and colleagues weighed cost against health gain for a three drug mix in advanced cervical cancer in China. The mix adds two targeted drugs to standard chemotherapy. Using trial survival data, they built a model that follows patients in three week steps over ten years and counts costs, years lived, and quality adjusted years.

The mix added about half a quality adjusted year, but at a very high extra cost. Cost per added quality year came to many times what China counts as good value. Extra checks on uncertain inputs did not change the verdict. From a public payer view, the authors conclude the mix does not give value for money at current prices.
plos-pone-0351129:
Shahadul Hassan Sourav and colleagues used computer modelling to hunt for plant compounds that could block two weapons of Listeria, a foodborne germ that can kill. One weapon helps the germ enter human cells, the other helps it burst out and spread. From a library of over twelve hundred plant flavonoids, docking tests ranked which compounds grip each weapon best.

Top compounds passed drug likeness and safety screens, then held steady in long molecular motion simulations. Detailed energy checks backed the stability of the best pairs. No cells or animals were tested, so the work is a shortlist, not a treatment. Still, it points chemists to a few plant molecules worth making and testing in the lab.
plos-pone-0351229:
Big cities often run several railway stations at once. Planners must decide which trains use which station. Yidong Wang built a mathematical model for that decision. The model balances railway costs against passenger travel costs. It treats the whole hub as one routing problem. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

The model respects real limits. Lines and station tracks have fixed capacity. Each city zone generates its own demand. Trains can only make so many stops. A worked example tested the model on a typical hub. The optimized plan cost less than two comparison plans. Track use also spread more evenly. Practical advice for railway departments follows.
plos-pone-0351429:
Gene data can flag who faces higher disease risk, but hundreds of competing methods claim to pick the right genes. Wesley Fletcher and Samiran Sinha benchmarked many of them head to head, in this 2026 PLOS One study built on simulated datasets plus a public cancer collection.

The fake datasets varied in how sparse the signal was, how strongly genes moved together, and how loud the true markers were. Methods were scored on false alarms, on balanced detection, and on how well their risk models ranked patients and timed events. The authors offer the comparison as a guide for researchers choosing tools for survival data with missing end dates.
plos-pone-0351629:
Shalinie King and colleagues set up blood pressure checks inside a public dental clinic in Australia. High blood pressure often goes unnoticed, and poor mouth health has been linked with it. Over six months they measured pressure twice for just over three hundred adults and asked about health history, teeth, and gum care needs.

About half of visitors met the study mark for high blood pressure. Most of those affected knew their status and took medicine, yet only a bit over half of treated people had pressure under control. Older adults were far more likely to be affected. Younger adults were less likely to know or to be treated. A dental visit, the team notes, can catch cases that clinics miss.
plos-pone-0351729:
Feiping Xu and colleagues built a prediction model for traffic conditions on highways passing through roadworks, where lane patterns keep changing and ordinary forecasters lose the plot. Their network pairs a graph model of the road system with a dynamic Bayesian layer that redraws the map of which road segments influence each other as the work zone's layout shifts. Geometry and traffic organization changes feed in as first-class inputs.

Congestion forecasts matter beyond convenience: jammed traffic wastes fuel and fouls air around construction for months. A model that expects the road itself to be a moving target should hold accuracy where static models decay. The work is a methods contribution, tested on work-zone scenarios, offering traffic managers a tool designed for the exact conditions, rebuilding under live traffic, where their current forecasts are weakest.
plos-pone-0351929:
Erin Grabarczyk and Jason Schmidt used DNA in spider gut contents to compare the menu of the introduced Joro spider with three native orb-weavers in the southeastern United States. The Joro, a large Asian species spreading fast, might compete with natives for prey or eat them. Samples came from female spiders at fifty-two sites inside the invader's new range.

Many prey kinds appeared in both the Joro and the natives, yet the overall makeup of their diets differed clearly. Joro meals stood apart in composition rather than simply copying the natives' menu. Diets of natives also shifted at sites shared with Joro spiders. For ecologists gauging invasion damage, gut DNA gives a finer picture than watching webs and guessing who eats what.
plos-pone-0352029:
Satoshi Komatsu and colleagues tested a new kind of bedside X-ray in intensive care. The method films the lungs while they move. It uses little radiation and shows the diaphragm in real time. The team asked whether it could flag patients likely to worsen after a breathing tube comes out. Fifty-six adults were filmed just before the tube came out and again within a day.

The filmed measures did not separate patients who worsened from those who did not. Age and breathing rate before removal did separate them. The authors call the work exploratory, and they mean it. A first look like this still guides the next study. Motion images may need to join plain clinical signs before they can predict well.
plos-pone-0352129:
Ryadul Alam and co-authors surveyed university students in Dhaka about fear of missing out, phone addiction, and mental health. Heavy phone dependence creates fresh psychological risks for young adults. Their 2026 cross-sectional study questioned five hundred undergraduates at public and private universities with standardised Bangla scales.

Over half of students reported a moderate fear of missing out, and about one in five met the study's bar for smartphone addiction. Distress was widespread: most reported depressive symptoms, and over half reported extremely severe anxiety. Alam and colleagues set out to test how tightly the fear of missing out predicts addiction and distress, arguing campuses should treat the trio as one connected problem.
plos-pone-0352329:
Shultz and colleagues combined three watching tools at wind turbines in Iowa in a 2026 study. Turbines share the sky with migrating birds and bats, but each common survey tool catches only part of that traffic. Over thirty-eight fall nights, the team ran heat cameras, bat sound recorders, and weather radar at two inland turbines.

More than twelve thousand flight paths were tracked at blade height, alongside thousands of bat calls and a huge radar count of passing birds. Heat camera counts rose and fell with radar traffic, but not with bat calls. That pattern suggests most camera tracks were birds on busy migration nights. Layering the tools gives a fuller picture of risk than any one of them alone.
plos-pone-0353029:
Hernández Bolio and colleagues, in a 2026 archaeology study, read the diets of Classic-period Maya commoners from the chemistry of their bones and teeth. The work covers southeastern Petén, in today's Guatemala, a region of many small rival centers rather than one great city, where no diet study of this kind had been done. Samples came from non-elite burials across more than four hundred recorded sites.

Carbon and nitrogen traces in bone, plus carbon in tooth enamel, point to diets built on maize, rounded out with other plants and land animals. Details varied between sites, tracking local ecology and custom, and varied by age as well. Reliance on maize grew toward the end of the Classic period and beyond. The authors compare their commoners with published city dwellers elsewhere in the Maya world, and argue that even in a politically scattered land, maize bound daily life together.
plos-pone-0353429:
Murshed and colleagues tested plant extracts against a pigeon gut parasite in a 2026 study. Cinnamon and bay laurel are rich in phenols and aromatic oils with known germ-fighting power. Extracts were measured for plant compounds, checked for antioxidant strength, and tried on parasite eggs at seven strengths.

Lab assays gauged whether the extracts could stop eggs from developing, a step that spreads disease between birds. Antioxidant tests used standard radical-fighting measures. Natural options matter because drug resistance and residue worries limit chemical treatments in food animals. Early dish results cannot prove field benefit, but they mark which extracts deserve animal trials.
plos-pone-0353529:
Bustos and colleagues, in a 2026 study, put volunteer firefighters on a treadmill to check whether their fitness matches the demands of the job. Firefighting calls for hard bursts of effort, and national guidance sets a floor for oxygen capacity. Thirty-one male volunteers ran in steps of rising speed, with short rests, while their breathing, heart rate, and blood markers were tracked.

As speed rose, oxygen use, heart rate, and energy burn all climbed steeply, and the body leaned more on fast, oxygen-free energy. About half of the men did not reach the age-based oxygen threshold that fire standards recommend. Heavier men showed lower heart rates at hard intensities, a pattern the authors discuss rather than celebrate. The message is plain: goodwill is not fitness, and volunteer brigades need structured training and testing if members are to meet the strain of real fires safely.
plos-pone-0354029:
Dodek and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, treat drug dosing as a design problem rather than trial and error. A pill taken repeatedly should hold its effect in a target band: too little fails, too much harms. Bodies absorb and clear drugs in nonlinear ways that standard recipes handle loosely. The authors build an optimization framework around that reality.

Each dose is modeled as a pulse entering a chain of body compartments, and the effect follows a standard S-shaped response curve. The team derives how the effect shifts when dose size or the pill's release rate changes, which lets a classic solver tune both at once. In computer tests with a four-compartment body model, the tuned regimen reached the target effect quickly, held it steady over many cycles, and swung less between doses. The work is in silico, a mathematical rehearsal meant to guide real formulation design.
plos-pone-0354129:
Liu and Rong, in a 2026 study, propose a new way to measure how interdisciplinary a research paper is, and test whether breadth helps a paper get cited. Old measures count the spread of a paper's references across fields, which can miss whether ideas truly blend. Their measure reads the text itself, using a language model to place each paper in a meaning space.

More than one hundred twenty thousand papers across all major fields, from 2015 to 2025, were scored. The new measure agreed moderately with the old ones and added a small amount of extra explanatory power. Public hospital nurses face heavy demands with thin resources, a classic burnout recipe. Their 2026 analysis used a demands-and-resources lens on questionnaires from just over two hundred nurses.

Average burnout sat a little above the scale's midpoint. Heavier workload tracked strongly with higher burnout. Mindfulness, the habit of present-moment attention, tracked with lower burnout. So did a relationship-oriented ward culture, where teamwork and trust are prized. Together the model explained well over half the differences between nurses. Chang and Jin argue managers should cut load and build culture, not only counsel individuals.
plos-pone-0355229:
Terri Flood and three others design a program to help British teenagers decide for themselves about HPV vaccination, in this 2026 study from Northern Ireland. The vaccine is normally offered at twelve or thirteen with parents deciding, but unvaccinated students can self-consent later, and mid-adolescence, when sexual activity typically begins, is a natural second chance. Working through a structured behavior-change framework, the team reviewed prior work and consulted immunization nurses, teachers, and the teenagers themselves.

They mapped twelve barriers across three targets: students deciding, staff delivering, and public attitudes warming. The resulting package pairs school-based HPV education, aligned with mandated curriculum changes and an actual vaccination opportunity, with a public media campaign, and specifies who should deliver it and how. The authors note success needs backing from health and education authorities, and they propose a feasibility pilot next.
plos-pone-0355729:
Ji Huang and colleagues designed a hybrid artificial intelligence model to predict diabetes that first appears in pregnancy. Gestational diabetes threatens mothers and newborns, so early warning matters. Their 2026 model fuses routine clinical measures with genetic features, weighting each source by how the two relate.

A sliding window step rebuilds individual records into group-aware sequences, letting the model see both personal risk and population patterns. Two architectures share the work: one built for efficient sequence reading, one transformer for wider context. Training used a public competition dataset from a Chinese cloud platform. plos-pone-0355829:

Their system reads nearly two decades of records from a Chinese ecology station and selects a score of physically meaningful measures, including core parts of a standard fire weather index. A layered network then reads patterns at several time scales and blends them for the forecast.

Against seven rival models, the new forecaster cut average error sharply and explained fire risk far better. It also traced the risk path of Australia's catastrophic fire season with striking accuracy despite training far away. Chen and colleagues present the physics-guided design as a template for fire agencies that need warnings grounded in how fires actually behave.
plos-pone-0356529:
Moritz Knoche and six colleagues characterize a blemish disorder of the Cosmic Crisp apple, sold as WA 38, in this 2026 study. Green spots that later brown and sink into the skin hurt the fruit's market value. The team followed developing fruit through the season, from the first green halos around the skin's pores, called lenticels, to cracking, and compared skin inside and outside the spots in fine detail.

Nearly all spots centered on lenticels, and bagged fruit, shielded on the tree, never developed them. Skin within spots showed strained, thickened cuticle, smaller cells, chemical signs of damage, and faster water loss. The authors conclude these skin changes are the disorder's footprint, not its trigger: the underlying cause seems to be localized restriction of surface growth, which stretches the skin until it reacts. Recruitment ran across much of a recent year, and the questionnaire asked about supplement use, other habits for keeping levels up, and where people get their information.

Being female, higher income, having a chronic disease, having been tested, and knowing deficiency symptoms each tracked with use. Sun exposure and vitamin-rich food were the most common maintenance habits, and the internet rivaled clinics as an information source. The authors offer the map for regional deficiency campaigns.
plos-pone-0357829:

When blood flow returns after being cut off, the injury can stiffen muscles into contractures. Using a rat leg model where the main artery was clamped and released, they traced damage to oxidative stress, reactive oxygen that scars DNA and kills muscle cells. They then tested whether a common antioxidant drug, N-acetylcysteine, could block the chain.

After blood flow returned, both calf muscles showed oxidative DNA damage, rising cell death, and accumulating collagen, the stiff scar protein behind contractures. Giving the antioxidant sharply reduced all three. In dish-grown muscle cells, hydrogen peroxide switched on death and fibrosis signals, and the antioxidant reversed those too. The authors suggest a cheap, familiar drug might one day be given around replantation surgery to protect function, though human use would need trials.
plos-pone-0358129:

Heuler's protocol uses healthy volunteers whose lower back pain is induced in a safe, mechanical way. Sensors will record how they move during set tasks, and fear measures will be read beside the motion data. plos-pone-0358229:
