propertius-elegies-butler-loeb-1929:
Sextus Propertius poured his stormy love for a woman he calls Cynthia into four books of elegies in the age of Augustus. H. E. Butler translated the poems into plain prose for the Loeb series. His version gives the complete Cynthia cycle, from first sight to bitter end.

Propertius is the most allusive voice of Augustan poetry: every love scene drags in gods, myths, and old wars. The last book turns to Rome itself, its rites, its dead heroes, and a ghost who speaks from the tomb. Butler's prose lets English readers follow the dense Latin line by line. The poems set the mold for love elegy after him.
proust-captive-moncrieff-1929:
The Captive, fifth volume of In Search of Lost Time, was published in French in 1923, after Marcel Proust's death. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation came out in 1929. The narrator now keeps Albertine in his Paris rooms, half guest and half prisoner, while jealousy eats at him daily.

He watches her sleep, questions her friends, and fears her secret past. Albertine, bored and trapped, plans her escape from his control. Their locked rooms become a study of love turned into surveillance. Proust stretches single days across hundreds of pages of fine attention. The volume is his fullest study of jealousy as a form of knowledge.
razi-de-aluminibus-et-salibus-steele-192:
The Book of Alums and Salts bears the name of al-Razi, the Persian doctor and alchemist who died in 925. Gerard of Cremona turned it into Latin in the twelfth century, and Robert Steele gave it English form in the journal Isis in 1929. It is the first Western work on making chemical substances ready for use.

Salt by salt and alum by alum, the book tells how to clean, roast, dissolve, and test each material. The tone is that of a workshop bench book, not a book of secrets. Such plain craft writing carried Arabic chemistry into Latin Europe. Steele's version keeps the matter close for students of the early craft.
remarque-all-quiet-1929: Remarque's 1929 All Quiet on the Western Front follows German soldiers in the trenches. It exposed war's lie. The Tower library holds the full text. It showed the mud. Boys died. Myths broke. Truth bled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
remy-demonolatry-1929:
Nicolas Remy feeds the flames with law in Demonolatry, here in the English text of 1929. Remy was a high law man in Lorraine who boasted he had sent scores on scores of witches to death: nine score in all, by the lore of his book of 1595. Ashwin turned the Latin to English, with notes by Montague Summers, for this late print of the grim work.

Remy sets out the sabbath, the pact, and wolf turns as points of law. His pride in the count is the book's true horror. It is the hunt's creed.
rise-of-the-new-west-1819-1829: Frederick Jackson Turner's Rise of the New West covers America from 1819 to 1829. The rough frontier democracy of Andrew Jackson's age takes shape in these pages. Sectional quarrels, new states, and western settlement fill the stirring story. A true classic of American historical writing.
roosevelt-trailing-the-giant-panda-1929:
Theodore Roosevelt the younger and his brother Kermit rode into China in 1929 to fetch a fabled bear. Trailing the Giant Panda tells of the hunt for the giant panda, the mystery bear of the border hills. No Westerner had yet brought one out of the wild.

The brothers cross hard country, track the shy beast by its sign, and at last bring one down. Their panda reached the West as proof the tales were true. The book is a brisk tale of camp, trail, and sportsmanship. It also marks the hour the panda stepped from rumor into the world's zoos.
russell-marriage-morals-1929:
Marriage and Morals, published in 1929, was Russell's most controversial book on social questions. It argues that the sexual morality of his day, built on fear and ignorance, damaged marriages and warped children's lives.

Russell defends sex education, easier divorce, and tolerance for unions outside marriage, and he questions whether strict monogamy serves most couples. The book scandalized Britain and America; a decade later it was used to bar him from a New York professorship. Views then called prophetic now read as temperate. The scandal is history, and the argument can finally be heard on its merits.
sarpi-council-of-trent-1629:
Paolo Sarpi, a Venetian friar and adviser, wrote his Istoria del Concilio Tridentino in 1619 as a secret history of the Council of Trent. The council had remade the Catholic Church in answer to the Reformation, and Sarpi, no friend of Rome, told how it really worked. His manuscript was smuggled out of Venice for printing, and Nathaniel Brent's English translation appears here in the 1629 printing.

Sarpi shows pope, bishops, and princes bargaining behind the council's solemn face. His case is that Rome bent a church council to its own power. The book became the great anti-papal history of the council, checked and fought over ever since. Few works of history carried such risk to their maker.
swift-modest-proposal-1729:
Jonathan Swift published A Modest Proposal anonymously in Dublin in 1729. Ireland was starving under English trade rules and landlord neglect, and Swift had spent years writing angry pamphlets about it. This pamphlet pretends to be calm economic advice from a helpful planner.

The proposer, with tables and figures, suggests that poor Irish families sell their babies as food for the rich. Swift keeps the tone reasonable while the horror builds line by line. The real targets are the landlords, officials, and economists whose policies already treated the Irish as less than human. The work is the most famous satire in English and still shocks new readers.
thomson-narrative-life-medical-discoveri:
Thomson told his own story in A Narrative of the Life and Medical Discoveries, printed in 1829. The New Hampshire farmer traces his path from sickly youth to founder of a healing system. He recalls watching his mother's illness, testing plants on himself, and slowly building his method.

Trials, rivals, and charges of harm fill the later chapters, and Thomson answers them all as persecution. He presents his vindication as proof that nature's remedies beat learned medicine. The book reads as both memoir and manifesto, the founding document of the Thomsonian movement in its maker's own words.
thucydides-peloponnesian-war-hobbes-1629:
Thucydides wrote his History of the Peloponnesian War in Greek, and Thomas Hobbes Englished it in 1629. Hobbes's was the first English Thucydides made straight from the Greek text of the history. The translator later wrote Leviathan, and his hard political sense suits this hard history well.

Athens and Sparta fight a long war that grinds Greece down over twenty-seven years. Speeches state each side's case with cold logic, from Pericles to the Melian dialogue's threats. Plague at Athens and the Sicilian disaster mark the arc of imperial overreach and fall. Thucydides claims no fables, only what men did and why power moved them to act. Hobbes prized him as the most political writer who ever lived in Greece.

Herbert Giles translated the writings of Chuang Tzu, the most playful of the Taoist classics. Chuang Tzu tells stories and spins paradoxes rather than laying down rules. In the most famous, he dreams he is a butterfly, then wonders whether the butterfly is now dreaming him.

Talking skulls, useless trees that survive because nobody can use them, and a butcher whose blade never dulls carry the teaching. Rigid distinctions between big and small, useful and useless, life and death dissolve as the tales turn. Readers who find Laozi severe will find Chuang Tzu funny, strange, and quietly radical about going along with the way of things.
tob-10829:
H. P. Blavatsky explained her own system in The Key to Theosophy in 1889, choosing plain question-and-answer form. An imaginary inquirer asks, and Blavatsky replies: What is Theosophy? What happens after death? Who are the mahatmas? How should a Theosophist live? The movement's official primer was written to settle confusion.

Dialogue lets her correct popular misunderstandings one by one, including charges that Theosophy is Buddhism in disguise or a new religion. The tone is direct, sometimes combative, but the structure stays clear. V1 evidence recommends starting here before tackling The Secret Doctrine, advice a century of readers has confirmed by experience.
tob-4029:
Adam Smith published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776, the year America declared independence. The book founded economics as a discipline. Its opening example, the pin factory, shows the division of labor multiplying output, and its argument builds from workshops to whole trading nations.

Markets coordinate self-interest toward public benefit, in Smith's famous image, as if by an invisible hand, while monopolies and tariffs draw his sustained attack. Smith is subtler than his later slogans: he assigns government real duties in defense, justice, and public works. Nations still govern, and argue, inside the frame this book built.
tob-4129:
Mead wrote Fragments of a Faith Forgotten in 1900 to rescue the Gnostics from the reports of their enemies. Valentinus, Basilides, and Marcion receive fair hearings as thinkers, not mere heretics. Short sketches build a picture of the second century's wildest Christian movements.

Mead reads the fragments with sympathy and a scholar's care, asking what the Gnostics meant before asking where they erred. The book made Gnosticism a modern subject of study rather than a footnote of abuse. Verified from the 1919 edition, it remains the work that taught occult and academic readers alike to take the heretics seriously.
travels-ibn-battuta-lee-1829:
Samuel Lee translated The Travels of Ibn Batuta into English in 1829 for the Oriental Translation Committee. It was the first English rendering of the Rihla, drawn from an Arabic abridgment. Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan scholar, left home in 1325 for the pilgrimage to Mecca and did not settle again for nearly thirty years.

His road ran some seventy-five thousand miles, from Morocco to China and from Anatolia to East Africa. Courts, shrines, plagues, and shipwrecks fill his plain, curious record. He served sultans as judge in Delhi and the Maldives along the way. Lee's version gave English readers the greatest traveler of the medieval world. No other medieval journey covers so much of the earth.
un-ga-res-29: Scheduling, not war or peace, fills Resolution 29 of the General Assembly, passed on 9 February 1946. Urgent questions were already before the new UN bodies, which would keep working between sessions. The text rules that the sitting session will pause in February and count as the first part of the first regular session. The second part would open in September, with the new headquarters work in the meantime.
un-ga-res-a-69-29:
A Middle East free of nuclear arms has been the Assembly's stated goal since the 1970s, and Resolution A/69/29 renews the call. The text recalls the chain of votes back to 1974. All states of the region are urged to take the swift, workable steps the plan needs. Till the zone stands, they should pledge in solemn form to make, get, or hold no nuclear arms.

No third party should be let to base such arms on their soil. All atomic plants in the region should sit under the checks of the world atomic body. Pledges to that end should be lodged with the Security Council. The ban on attacks on atomic plants is stressed as well.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, General Assembly Resolution 29 It set the calendar of the first session. It voted to meet again on the first Tuesday after 2 September 1946, for the second part.

General Assembly resolution 69/29 (2014) is the Assembly's annual call for a nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Middle East, a proposal it has backed by consensus since 1980. It urges the region's states to take practical steps toward the zone. It urges them to join the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It urges them to place all nuclear activities under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards. Meanwhile they should refrain from developing or hosting nuclear weapons. The Secretary-General is asked to keep consulting the region's states and to report to the seventieth session.
un-sc-res-1029:
UNAMIR was wound down to its final months on 12 December 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 1 December set out the mission's state. Rwanda's foreign minister had written in August and November about the government's terms. Elements of the old regime were arming in the camps across the border, the Council noted with concern. Refugee return in safety and true reconciliation were the stated goals.

The Council extended UNAMIR's mandate for a final period, to 8 March 1996. The mandate was adjusted to stress help for refugee repatriation and for the government's rebuilding work. Troop strength would fall to 1,200, and military observers and support staff to 200. The civilian police part would be withdrawn. The Secretary-General had to start planning the full pullout once the mandate ended. He was also to study handing the mission's non-lethal gear to Rwanda's government.
un-sc-res-129: Lebanon and Jordan are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 129, adopted unanimously on 7 August 1958. Both states had complained of outside interference. American troops had landed in Lebanon and British troops in Jordan. Vetoes at two earlier meetings had blocked the Council from acting. Finding itself unable to carry out its chief duty for peace, the Council calls an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The move hands the crisis to the full membership. That session later backed steps meant to speed the foreign troops home.
un-sc-res-1329:
The war crimes tribunals are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1329, adopted on 30 November 2000. The tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda had heavy case loads. Their presidents asked for more judges so trials could end sooner. Both courts had also improved the way they worked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amends both statutes. It creates a pool of twenty-seven temporary judges for the Yugoslavia tribunal. The shared appeals chamber grows for both courts. Two extra judges will be elected for the Rwanda tribunal, and two of its judges will sit on appeals. Leaders, the text notes, should face trial before these courts rather than minor actors.
un-sc-res-1429:
Lack of progress on Western Sahara worried the Council in the summer of 2002. On 30 July 2002 it called a political solution critically needed. The deadlock caused suffering in the territory. It also risked unrest in the region. Trade and growth across the Maghreb suffered too. The Council wanted prisoners freed and the fate of missing people settled.

The text backs the Secretary-General and his envoy in full. It asks the parties and nearby states to cooperate with them. It urges work with the United Nations refugee agency on trust-building steps. Family visits between divided Sahrawi families were one such step. The referendum mission, MINURSO, kept its role while talks were sought.
un-sc-res-1529:
Resolution 1529 answered Haiti's February 2004 crisis, when armed revolt spread and President Jean-Bertrand Aristide left the country. The Security Council allowed member states to send a multinational force at once. Its job was to restore order and protect relief work.

Inside the text, the Council welcomes the new interim leadership and demands an end to violence against civilians. The foreign force was a bridge, meant to hold the country until a longer UN mission could take over. The resolution captures Haiti at a breaking point, with the world stepping in.
un-sc-res-1629: Resolution 1629 was adopted on October 3, 2005, according to its record, and is kept here in a Wikisource transcription. Short formal texts like this one often handle the Council's housekeeping of world affairs in a few paragraphs. The entry preserves the complete act, from the members' opening findings to the operative decisions that close it.
un-sc-res-1729: Resolution 1729, adopted in 2006, is a Security Council act kept here as a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. Routine renewals and urgent orders share its format, which is part of its interest. The entry shows the format plainly: grounds recited, prior texts recalled, and then the Council's decision set down in numbered order.
un-sc-res-1829:
Sierra Leone's integrated office was remade as a peacebuilding office on 4 August 2008. UNIOSIL had served the country's recovery well, the Council said. Peaceful local elections in July 2008 marked a fresh milestone. The Secretary-General's report of 29 April advised the new shape. The peacebuilding cooperation framework with the Peacebuilding Commission was moving forward.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to establish the United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, from 1 October 2008. It would run for an initial twelve months, succeeding UNIOSIL. The office had to focus on backing the government in peace consolidation and growth. A fully integrated United Nations team, with a single voice, was underlined. Close work with ECOWAS and other partners was stressed. The government bore the main duty for the country's peace and security, the Council said. All Sierra Leonean leaders were called to guard the calm the country had won.
un-sc-res-1929:
Resolution 1929, adopted in June 2010, was the toughest round of UN sanctions placed on Iran over its nuclear program. Iran had enriched uranium to a higher level and hidden a new site near Qom. The Council answered with broad new restrictions.

The text bans sales of major weapons to Iran, targets its Revolutionary Guard and shipping lines, and allows cargo inspections on the high seas. It also expands the lists of people and firms facing frozen assets. The resolution marked the peak of world pressure on Tehran before the diplomacy that led to the 2015 nuclear deal.
un-sc-res-2029:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 2029 concerns the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. The Council adopted it on 21 December 2011. The tribunal, set up after the 1994 genocide, was racing to finish its trials before closing. A new residual body was due to take over its leftover work in July 2012.

The text extends the terms of four permanent judges and eight temporary judges to 30 June 2012. They stay until that date or until their trials end, if sooner. The Council urges states to help arrest the last fugitives still at large. It also presses states to accept people who were cleared or who finished their prison terms.
un-sc-res-229: U Thant's first term as Secretary-General was ending in 1966. On 2 December 1966 the Security Council met in private to judge his record. It praised his proven qualities and high sense of duty. His reappointment, the Council said, would best serve the organization's larger interests. It therefore recommended that the General Assembly appoint him for another term. The short text is the Council's formal part in choosing the world's top official. U Thant served until the end of 1971.
un-sc-res-29: Two new states won the Security Council's blessing in Resolution 29 of 1947. A Council team had weighed a long list of bids for UN membership. Some were fresh looks at old bids: Albania, Mongolia, Transjordan, Ireland, and Portugal. Others were new: Hungary, Italy, Romania, Austria, Yemen, and Bulgaria. Pakistan's fresh bid was weighed as well. Of all these, the Council urges the General Assembly to admit just two: Yemen and Pakistan.
un-sc-res-329: Entered in the record as Resolution 329, this Security Council text is catalogued at 1968. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-429:
On the Golan Heights, United Nations observers kept watch between Israel and Syria. On 31 May 1978 the Security Council renewed their mission, UNDOF, for six more months. The Secretary-General had reported on the force. The Council noted efforts toward a just and durable peace in the Middle East. It also voiced concern at the tension that still hung over the area.

The new term ran until 30 November 1978. The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 at once. That 1973 text demanded a ceasefire and peace talks. The Secretary-General had to report at the term's end. One Council member, China, did not take part in the vote.
un-sc-res-829:
Security Council Resolution 829, adopted on May 26, 1993, recommended Monaco for membership in the United Nations. The small principality on the French Riviera, ruled by the Grimaldi family for centuries, had long handled its foreign ties through France. By the 1990s it sought a direct voice of its own in the world body.

The Assembly admitted Monaco two days later. Monaco's size raised a gentle question the council set aside: how small can a member be? The vote answered that statehood and acceptance of the Charter, not size, set the bar. The brief resolution thus widened the UN's claim to speak for states of every scale.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1029, adopted on 12 December 1995, sets the final chapter for the UN Assistance Mission for Rwanda, UNAMIR. The mission had been created in 1993, before the genocide, and reshaped several times since. Reports told of armed buildups and raids into Rwanda by members of the former regime, while the safe return of refugees and true national healing stayed the Council's stated goals.

The Council extends UNAMIR for a final period until 8 March 1996, with a narrower job. The mission is to help refugees return home safely, aid the refugee agency's supply work, and guard the International Tribunal for Rwanda for the time being. Its troops drop to 1,200, with 200 observers and support staff. Planning for a full pullout within six weeks after the mandate ends is ordered.

Deadlock in the Council during a Middle East crisis produced Resolution 129. It was adopted unanimously on 7 August 1958. At two recent meetings, the permanent members had split. That split stopped the Council from doing its main job: guarding international peace and security. The agenda items before it could not move.

The members therefore handed the problem upward. They decided to call an emergency special session. The General Assembly, with every member state voting, would take up the matter. This was the same escape route used over Hungary in 1956. It let the wider membership speak when vetoes froze the Council.

The war-crimes tribunals are enlarged by Resolution 1329, adopted unanimously on 30 November 2000. Both tribunals — for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda — faced long dockets, and their presidents had asked for more judges so trials could finish sooner. The Council also took the view that senior leaders, not minor actors, should be the tribunals' priority.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a pool of ad litem judges for the Yugoslavia tribunal. The pool holds 27 judges elected by the General Assembly, assigned to trials as needed for up to three years each. It enlarges the shared Appeals Chambers of both tribunals and orders two additional judges elected for the Rwanda tribunal, two of whose judges will sit on the Appeals Chambers. The statutes of both tribunals are amended by annexes to the resolution. A report on ending the Yugoslavia tribunal's temporal jurisdiction is also requested.

Stalemate itself is the subject of this Sahara text of 2002. On 30 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1429 without dissent. It stressed that the lack of progress was a grave concern. The territory's people kept suffering for it. The whole region faced the risk of unrest. The Maghreb's growth stayed blocked as well.

The Council had weighed the Secretary-General's February report. Four options for the territory sat in that report. The old vote plan stays valid, the text underlines. Deep gaps between the parties over it are noted all the same. Strong backing goes to the Secretary-General and his envoy. Their hunt for a political deal both sides can accept must press on.

Haiti's political, security, and humanitarian situation had collapsed into violence when this text passed on 29 February 2004. The country's president had resigned, and an acting president sworn in under the constitution appealed for urgent outside support. An emergency force is the Council's answer.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the immediate deployment of a Multinational Interim Force for no more than three months. Its tasks are to help restore order, support the constitutional process, protect human rights, and let aid workers reach people in need. States are called on to supply troops, equipment, and money at once. A longer-term United Nations force, the Council signals, will follow.

A narrow staffing decision for the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is made on 30 September 2005. Judge Christine Van Den Wyngaert had been elected a permanent judge, but her term was not due to start until 17 November 2005. The Council assigned her early, as a permanent judge, to the Mrksic case, which was due to open on 3 October 2005. The usual timing rules in the tribunal's Statute were set aside for this purpose.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed for six months on 15 December 2006, until 30 June 2007. UNDOF continues its watch between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. A closing report on developments is asked for.

Resolution 1829, adopted on 4 August 2008, reshapes the UN presence in Sierra Leone once more. Calm local elections had been held in July 2008, and the army and police were growing more skilled. The earlier integrated office, UNIOSIL, was ending, and the Peacebuilding Commission was now working with the government on long-term needs.

The Council asks for a new United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, for twelve months from 1 October 2008. Its work covers easing tensions before they turn into conflict. It also covers watching human rights and the rule of law. It backs the fight against corruption. It supports local government and a review of the 1991 constitution. The office must work closely with the Peacebuilding Commission, ECOWAS, and the Mano River Union. Reports are due every four months.

On 9 June 2010 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1929, a fourth round of sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program. The Council said Iran had still not met the demands of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Iran had not suspended its sensitive nuclear work. The text also reaffirmed the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

The new measures banned the sale to Iran of heavy weapons. The list covered tanks, combat aircraft, attack helicopters, and warships. Iran was barred from investing abroad in uranium mining and enrichment work. States were told to inspect suspect cargo and to block activity linked to missiles. They also had to watch dealings with Iranian banks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Long lists at the end name the companies and bodies placed under the sanctions.

Resolution 2029, adopted on 21 December 2011, keeps judges of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in post as the court heads toward closure. The tribunal was told to finish all work by 31 December 2014 and hand over to the International Residual Mechanism, whose Rwanda branch would start on 1 July 2012. Finding new homes for acquitted people and those who had finished their sentences remained a problem.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the terms of four permanent trial judges and eight ad litem judges until 30 June 2012, or until their trials end. It presses UN bodies to help the tribunal keep the staff it needs. It urges all states to help catch and hand over the remaining fugitives. It praises states that have taken in acquitted people or those who finished their sentences, and asks others to do the same.

Keeping U Thant in office is the business of Resolution 229, adopted at a private meeting on 2 December 1966. The Burmese diplomat had served as Secretary-General since 1961, steering the United Nations through the Congo crisis and other Cold War strains. Council members praised his proven qualities and high sense of duty.

The Council recommends his appointment for another term, saying his return would serve the organization best. Under the Charter, the General Assembly makes the appointment, but only on the Council's recommendation. U Thant accepted a second term that ran until the end of 1971, making this short text part of the record of his decade leading the UN.

Applications to join the United Nations came back before the Council in 1947. A committee on new members had looked again at a long list of bids, from countries in Europe and beyond. Resolution 29 records the result of that review. The Council weighed the views its members had stated on each application. In the end it recommended to the General Assembly that two applicants be admitted: Yemen and Pakistan. The other bids in the round did not win the Council's backing at that time.

Zambia decided in 1973 to stop sending its trade along the southern route through Rhodesia. The boycott would last until the rebellion there ended and majority rule was established. The step backed the Council's sanctions, but it strained Zambia's economy. A special mission had reported on Zambia's urgent needs. Resolution 329 was adopted unanimously on 10 March 1973.

The Council praised Zambia's decision. It appealed to all states for immediate help. Technical, financial, and material aid were all requested. United Nations bodies were asked to organize assistance at once. Trade and development agencies were among those named. The help would let Zambia keep its traffic moving by other routes. It would also build Zambia's economic independence from the racist regime in Rhodesia.

The Golan watch rolled on with this renewal of 1978. On 31 May, the Council adopted Resolution 429. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China took no part in the vote. The Secretary-General had reported on the observer force, UNDOF. The Council noted the push for a lasting Middle East peace. It voiced concern at the tension in the area.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. It renews the observer mandate for six months, to 30 November 1978. A closing report from the Secretary-General is due then. The vote came two months after the Council built a new force for Lebanon.

Monaco's seat at the United Nations begins with Resolution 829, adopted on 26 May 1993. The Council weighed the bid of Monaco, a principality filed as document S/25796. The tiny city-state on the French Riviera had long kept a limited international profile, relying on France for defense while running its own affairs.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Monaco to membership. The Assembly acted the same day, and Monaco took its seat. In the Assembly's one-state-one-vote system, the second-smallest country in the world votes as an equal of the largest. The resolution was adopted at the meeting right after the one recommending Eritrea, a busy week for admissions.
undset-the-snake-pit-olav-audunssn-i-192:
Olav Audunsson's story begins in The Snake Pit, the first book of Undset's second medieval saga, in Archer's 1929 English version. Olav, a landowner in thirteenth-century Norway, marries the woman he loves. She brings a hard secret into the marriage: a child by another man.

Honor, sin, and silence shape Olav's life from the wedding onward. Undset writes a sterner tale here than in the Kristin books. Love does not free her hero; it binds him to guilt and duty. Readers meet a man who will carry one dark choice for the rest of his days.
usama-ibn-munqidh-memoirs-hitti-1929:
Usama ibn Munqidh, a Syrian prince of the castle of Shayzar, fought the Crusaders, hunted with falcons, and served the courts of Damascus and Cairo. Late in life he wrote the Kitab al-I'tibar, the Book of Learning by Example. Philip Hitti translated it into English in 1929. It is the great personal memoir of the Crusader age from the Muslim side.

Usama tells of battles, sieges, hunts, and doctors, and of his odd friendships with Frankish knights. His tales of Frankish medicine and justice are famous, told with dry wonder. He writes as a man of eighty looking back on a world of war and courtesy. No other voice brings that age so close.
von-stein-mokele-mbembe-bolsche-1929:
A German trek brings back a tale of a live dinosaur in the report set in print by Wilhelm Bolsche in 1929. Bolsche quotes the notes of von Stein, who led a trek through the Congo in 1913 and 1914. Tribes there told of a vast beast in the swamps and streams, with a long neck and a bulk like an elephant, that kills hippos yet eats no flesh at all.

Von Stein took the tales as grave and matched. No beast was seen by his men. The report is the root source for the beast since named mokele-mbembe. All hunts since start here.
waite-holy-kabbalah-1929:
Waite traced the secret tradition of Israel through two thousand years in The Holy Kabbalah of 1929. The massive study follows Jewish Kabbalah and its Christian heirs in the West. Waite wrote as both scholar and mystic, a rare mix in his field.

He treats the Zohar, the schools of Spain and Safed, and the Christian scholars who took the lore up. His care is to sift the record from the myth that clings to it. The book was the standard English survey of its subject for its age. Students of Christian Kabbalah still keep it close at hand.
walker-appeal-1829: Walker's 1829 Appeal urged enslaved Blacks to revolt for freedom. The South banned it. The Tower library holds the full text. It cried resistance. Chains bound. Words freed. Courage sparked. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
whitehead-aims-education-1929:
The Aims of Education, published in 1929, collects Whitehead's essays on education, universities, and the rhythm of learning. Its title essay gives his famous standard: education is the art of the utilization of knowledge.

Whitehead attacks inert ideas, knowledge received and never used, as the chief enemy of schooling. He proposes a rhythm for learning: romance, precision, and generalization, repeated at every stage. Other essays treat the place of classics, mathematics, and technical training. The book influenced generations of teachers and university planners. Its prose has the ease of a master summarizing a lifetime's thought about how minds grow.
whitehead-function-reason-1929:
The Function of Reason, published in 1929, prints Whitehead's Princeton lectures on a neglected question: what reason is for. Against the view of reason as a judge sitting above life, he presents it as an organ of fresh life within life itself.

Reason, Whitehead argues, promotes the art of life in three ways: to live, to live well, and to live better. He traces reason's work from animal appetites to science and the slow climb of civilized life. The lectures are brief, aphoristic, and humane. They distill the spirit of his process thought into a defense of speculation itself.
whitehead-process-reality-1929:
Process and Reality, published in 1929, is Whitehead's complete system, built from the Gifford Lectures he gave at Edinburgh in 1927 and 1928. Its subtitle calls it an essay in cosmology. It proposes that the world's basic units are not things but events, moments of experience.

Everything, from electrons to God, is process: becoming, perishing, and passing value into what follows. The terms he coins are famously hard, yet the vision is generous, a universe of feeling and fresh creation. The book founded process philosophy and later fed process theology. It is among the boldest works of its kind in English.
wolfe-look-homeward-angel-1929:
Thomas Wolfe was twenty-nine, a Harvard-trained playwright teaching in New York, when Look Homeward, Angel appeared in 1929. He had written the huge manuscript in a flood, and editor Maxwell Perkins cut it into shape. Wolfe set it in Altamont, his barely disguised Asheville, North Carolina.

Eugene Gant grows up in his mother's boardinghouse, the youngest of a stormy, gifted family. His father carves tombstone angels, his brother Ben dies young, and Eugene hungers for everything: books, women, cities, fame. Wolfe's prose pours out in torrents of memory and appetite, too much and unforgettable at once. Asheville recognized itself and was furious. The novel is the most exuberant debut in American fiction.
woolf-room-of-ones-own-1929:
Virginia Woolf published A Room of One's Own in 1929, growing from lectures she gave at Cambridge women's colleges in 1928. Woolf asked why so few women had written great literature. Her answer became a founding claim of feminist literary criticism.

A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction, Woolf argued. She imagined Shakespeare's sister, as gifted as her brother, crushed by a world that barred her from school and stage. Woolf traced women's writing from letters to novels as their material freedom grew. The essay's wit and anger still open courses on women and literature.
wurzburg-hexen-leut-verzeichnis-1629:
Names fill this 1629 print and little else: a list of the witch people burned at Würzburg. Verzeichnis der Hexen-Leut zu Würzburg names 157 men, women, and children put to the fire. The prince-bishop's hunt was then at its height in the German lands.

Clergy, councilors, wives, and young students stand in the roll beside the poor. Each line is one life ended by the court and the stake. The print was sold as news and warning in its own day. Few papers of the German hunts chill a reader more than this bare list.
